topics.title: Innate and adaptive immunity in rheumatic disease
mustKnow: Pattern recognition receptors include Toll-like receptors (TLRs) and NOD-like receptors. TLR4 recognises bacterial lipopolysaccharide and endogenous danger molecules such as HMGB1, whereas endosomal TLR7 and TLR9 recognise viral or self single-stranded RNA and unmethylated CpG DNA, driving type I interferon production in systemic lupus erythematosus.

The NLRP3 inflammasome consists of NLRP3, ASC adapter protein, and procaspase-1. Cleavage of procaspase-1 generates active caspase-1, which processes pro-IL-1beta and pro-IL-18 into their mature active secretory forms, a pivotal mechanism in gout, pseudogout, and cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes.

Naive CD4+ T helper differentiation is directed by lineage-specifying cytokines: IL-12 and IFN-gamma induce Th1 via T-bet, IL-4 induces Th2 via GATA3, whereas IL-6 and TGF-beta drive Th17 differentiation through transcription factor ROR-gamma-t, producing IL-17A, IL-17F, and IL-22 which drive neutrophilic tissue inflammation in spondyloarthritis.

Regulatory T cells express CD4, CD25, and transcription factor FOXP3. Defective FOXP3 function leads to the IPEX syndrome (immune dysregulation, polyendocrinopathy, enteropathy, X-linked), highlighting the non-redundant role of Tregs in suppressing autoreactive effector T cells via IL-10, TGF-beta, and contact-dependent CTLA-4.

Central B-cell tolerance in the bone marrow eliminates self-reactive immature B cells via clonal deletion or receptor editing of immunoglobulin light chains. Peripheral tolerance mechanisms include clonal anergy, functional suppression by regulatory B cells, and dependency on survival factor BAFF, excess of which promotes lupus autoimmunity.

Proinflammatory cytokines orchestrate articular damage: TNF-alpha and IL-6 promote synovial proliferation and osteoclastogenesis via RANKL induction. IL-23 stabilizes the Th17 phenotype, establishing the IL-23/IL-17 axis that underpins enthesitis and pathological new bone formation in spondyloarthropathies.

Genetic susceptibility across rheumatic diseases maps strongly to MHC loci: HLA-B27 confers a relative risk of over 40 for ankylosing spondylitis via peptide presentation, misfolding, or homodimer formation. Conversely, the shared epitope, a conserved pentapeptide sequence QKRAA or QRRAA in the HLA-DRB1 third hypervariable region, strongly predisposes to anti-CCP-positive rheumatoid arthritis.

Molecular mimicry occurs when microbial antigens share structural homology with self-peptides, triggering cross-reactive autoimmunity. The classic paradigm is group A streptococcal M protein evoking cross-reactive antibodies and cellular responses against cardiac myosin and basal ganglia in acute rheumatic fever.

topics.title: Autoantibodies and serological testing
mustKnow: Antinuclear antibody (ANA) testing by indirect immunofluorescence on HEp-2 cells is the gold standard screening test; a dilution of 1:160 or higher is recognized as clinically significant in the 2019 ACR/EULAR SLE classification criteria, yielding greater than 98% sensitivity.

Anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) antibodies demonstrate over 95% specificity for systemic lupus erythematosus, correlate with lupus nephritis disease activity, and activate complement, whereas anti-Smith (anti-Sm) antibodies are directed against core snRNP proteins and are virtually 99% specific for SLE but do not track with flare severity.

Anti-Ro/SSA (against Ro60 and Ro52) and anti-La/SSB antibodies associate with Sjogren syndrome and subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus; maternal transmission of anti-Ro/SSA antibodies across the placenta causes neonatal lupus, manifesting as congenital third-degree heart block in 2% of exposed pregnancies.

Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies have 95% to 98% specificity for rheumatoid arthritis, appear years before clinical synovitis, and portend aggressive erosive joint destruction, contrasting with rheumatoid factor (an IgM antibody directed against human IgG Fc portion) which has lower specificity and occurs in hepatitis C, subacute bacterial endocarditis, and normal elderly.

Cytoplasmic ANCA (c-ANCA) displays diffusely granular cytoplasmic staining on ethanol-fixed neutrophils, targets proteinase 3 (PR3), and is found in over 85% of active generalized granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA). Perinuclear ANCA (p-ANCA) targets myeloperoxidase (MPO) and is predominant in microscopic polyangiitis and eosinophilic GPA.

In systemic sclerosis, anti-centromere antibodies associate with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis and pulmonary arterial hypertension, whereas anti-topoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) denotes diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis and interstitial lung disease, and anti-RNA polymerase III correlates with diffuse scleroderma and scleroderma renal crisis.

Anti-Jo-1 (anti-histidyl-tRNA synthetase) is the archetypal antisynthetase antibody, identifying the syndrome of myositis, interstitial lung disease, Raynaud phenomenon, non-erosive arthritis, and mechanic's hands; other myositis-specific antibodies include anti-Mi-2 in classic dermatomyositis and anti-TIF1-gamma associated with malignancy.

Anti-ribosomal P antibodies display selective affinity for the carboxyl-terminal peptide of ribosomal proteins P0, P1, and P2; in systemic lupus erythematosus, anti-ribosomal P antibodies associate with psychiatric involvement, notably acute psychosis, depression, and severe hepatic involvement.

topics.title: Complement, acute phase reactants and immune complexes
mustKnow: The classical complement pathway is triggered by immune complexes binding C1q; profound congenital deficiency of early components (C1q, C1r, C1s, C4) carries an extraordinary risk of developing severe systemic lupus erythematosus exceeding 90% in homozygous C1q deficiency due to defective clearance of apoptotic debris.

The alternative complement pathway is initiated by spontaneous tick-over hydrolysis of C3 into C3(H2O) and stabilized on microbial surfaces by factor B and properdin; unchecked alternative pathway activity caused by autoantibodies against C3 convertase (C3 nephritic factor) leads to membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis and dense deposit disease.

Terminal complement components (C5b through C9) assemble into the membrane attack complex; inherited deficiencies of C5, C6, C7, C8, or C9 confer a markedly heightened susceptibility to recurrent disseminated infections with encapsulated Neisseria species (N. meningitidis and N. gonorrhoeae).

Depressed serum C3 and C4 levels reflect active immune complex-mediated consumption; profound hypocomplementemia characteristically accompanies active proliferative lupus nephritis, cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, and subacute bacterial endocarditis.

C-reactive protein (CRP) is a pentameric pattern recognition acute-phase protein synthesized by hepatocytes under direct stimulation by IL-6, with a short plasma half-life of 19 hours, making it an exquisite, rapid-responding indicator of systemic inflammation, bacterial infection, and treatment response.

Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) measures the settling velocity of erythrocytes and depends primarily on asymmetric plasma proteins, especially fibrinogen; a marked dissociation of high ESR with normal or low CRP is a classic diagnostic clue pointing toward active lupus flare, multiple myeloma, or severe hypergammaglobulinemia.

Extreme hyperferritinemia exceeding 10,000 ng/mL is an urgent diagnostic marker of macrophage activation syndrome (secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis), adult-onset Still disease, catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome, and severe septic shock with multiorgan failure.

Cryoglobulins are immunoglobulins that precipitate reversibly at temperatures below 37 degrees Celsius; Brouet classification stratifies them into Type I (isolated monoclonal Ig, associated with multiple myeloma and Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia), Type II (mixed monoclonal IgM with rheumatoid factor activity plus polyclonal IgG, linked to hepatitis C), and Type III (polyclonal IgM and IgG).

topics.title: Synovial fluid analysis and arthrocentesis
mustKnow: Arthrocentesis synovial fluid leukocyte count reliably categorizes joint effusions: normal fluid has fewer than 200 WBC/microL, non-inflammatory (osteoarthritis) ranges from 200 to 2,000 WBC/microL, inflammatory (rheumatoid arthritis, crystal arthropathies) spans 2,000 to 50,000 WBC/microL with greater than 50% neutrophils, and septic fluid typically exceeds 50,000 WBC/microL with greater than 75% polymorphs.

Under compensated polarized light microscopy with a red compensator, monosodium urate crystals appear needle-shaped with strong negative birefringence, displaying a brilliant yellow color when aligned parallel to the slow axis of the compensator and blue when perpendicular.

Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals are rhomboid or rod-shaped with weak positive birefringence under compensated polarized light, turning blue when parallel to the slow axis and yellow when perpendicular.

Basic calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite) crystals are ultramicroscopic and non-birefringent under light microscopy; identification requires transmission electron microscopy or alizarin red S staining which demonstrates globular clumping, characteristic of Milwaukee shoulder syndrome.

Hemarthrosis reveals grossly bloody or xanthochromic synovial fluid that does not clot if blood was intra-articular prior to aspiration; the presence of fat globules (lipid droplets floating on centrifuged supernatant) confirms an intra-articular fracture communicating with marrow.

Cholesterol crystals appear as large, flat, notched rectangular plates with moderate variable birefringence in chronically inflamed rheumatoid or tuberculous joint effusions, representing lipid breakdown products from chronic synovial tissue necrosis.

Synovial fluid Gram stain identifies organisms in 50% to 75% of non-gonococcal septic arthritis cases but in fewer than 25% of disseminated gonococcal infections, necessitating chocolate agar or Thayer-Martin culture and nucleic acid amplification testing.

Crystal-induced arthritis and true bacterial septic arthritis frequently coexist in the same joint effusion; discovering urate or CPPD crystals never excludes concomitant septic arthritis, and fluid must always undergo microbiological culture.

topics.title: Imaging in rheumatology
mustKnow: Musculoskeletal ultrasound (MSUS) detects subclinical synovitis and tenosynovitis with high sensitivity; power Doppler signal reflects active hypervascular synovial proliferation, correlating with ongoing structural damage in rheumatoid arthritis and guiding treat-to-target intensification.

The ultrasound double contour sign demonstrates a hyperechoic, irregular band over the superficial surface of hyaline cartilage, possessing greater than 90% specificity for monosodium urate crystal deposition in gout, distinct from cartilage calcification.

In spondyloarthritis, MRI of sacroiliac joints using short tau inversion recovery (STIR) or T2 fat-suppressed sequences identifies active inflammatory sacroiliitis by showing periarticular bone marrow edema, which is mandatory for the imaging arm of ASAS axial SpA criteria.

Dual-energy computed tomography (DECT) exploits differences in tissue attenuation at 80 kVp and 140 kVp to color-code and visualize monosodium urate crystal deposits with sensitivity and specificity exceeding 85% to 90%, proving invaluable for diagnosing tophaceous gout in atypical anatomical locations.

Conventional radiography in early rheumatoid arthritis shows periarticular osteopenia and soft tissue swelling, progressing to marginal cortical bone erosions at the bare areas (synovial reflection devoid of cartilage) of the second and third metacarpophalangeal and third proximal interphalangeal joints.

In ankylosing spondylitis, spinal radiography reveals vertebral body squaring, Romanus lesions (erosive shiny corners), and thin, delicate, vertically oriented syndesmophytes originating from the annulus fibrosus, resulting in classical bamboo spine, distinct from the thick, coarse, flowing horizontal osteophytes of DISH.

18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography with computed tomography (18F-FDG PET-CT) is the imaging modality of choice for detecting large vessel vasculitis (Takayasu arteritis and giant cell arteritis), demonstrating circumferential metabolic tracer uptake in the aorta and primary branches that exceeds hepatic uptake.

Nailfold capillaroscopy at 200x magnification detects microvascular architecture; the scleroderma pattern features giant capillary loops (diameter >50 micrometers), microhemorrhages, avascular areas, and neoangiogenic capillary arborization, distinguishing primary Raynaud from systemic sclerosis.

topics.title: Primary immunodeficiency disorders
mustKnow: X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton disease) results from mutations in Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK), leading to arrest of B-cell development at the pre-B stage; patients present after 6 months of age with profound panhypogammaglobulinemia, absence of mature CD19+ B cells in peripheral blood, absent tonsils, and recurrent sinopulmonary encapsulated bacterial infections.

Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) is the most frequent symptomatic primary immunodeficiency in adults, characterized by low IgG (at least 2 standard deviations below mean) plus low IgA or IgM, impaired vaccine antibody responses, recurrent infections, enteropathy, bronchiectasis, non-caseating granulomatous lymphocytic interstitial lung disease, and elevated lymphoma risk.

Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) represents a medical emergency caused by IL2RG mutations (X-linked) or adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency; infants present with failure to thrive, persistent thrush, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, and profound lymphopenia, requiring curative allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) arises from defects in NADPH oxidase subunits (gp91phox encoded by CYBB on X chromosome), abolishing the respiratory burst; patients suffer recurrent catalase-positive fungal and bacterial infections (Staphylococcus aureus, Burkholderia, Aspergillus, Serratia, Nocardia), diagnosed via dihydrorhodamine-123 (DHR) flow cytometry.

Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by WASP gene mutations, presenting with the classical triad of microthrombocytopenia with small platelets, eczema, and recurrent sinopulmonary and opportunistic infections, alongside heightened susceptibility to autoimmune hemolytic anemia and lymphoma.

Hyper-IgE syndrome (Job syndrome) is predominantly autosomal dominant caused by dominant-negative STAT3 mutations; hallmarks include extreme serum IgE levels exceeding 2,000 IU/mL, recurrent cold staphylococcal abscesses without classic inflammatory signs, pneumatoceles, coarse facial features, and retained primary teeth.

Terminal complement deficiencies (congenital absence of C5, C6, C7, C8, or C9) uniquely impair formation of the membrane attack complex, conferring a selective and life-threatening predisposition to recurrent, invasive, meningococcal and gonococcal Neisseria bacteremia, requiring meningococcal vaccination and prophylactic antibiotics.

Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) replacement therapy at a replacement dose of 400 to 600 mg/kg every 3 to 4 weeks or equivalent subcutaneous immunoglobulin (SCIG) is the life-saving standard of care in humoral immunodeficiencies (XLA and CVID) to maintain trough IgG levels above 700 to 800 mg/dL and prevent bronchiectasis.

topics.title: Acquired immunodeficiency and immune dysregulation
mustKnow: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection triggers paradoxical rheumatic and autoimmune syndromes including severe reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis flares, polymyositis, and diffuse infiltrative lymphocytosis syndrome (DILS), even in the face of progressive CD4+ T-cell depletion.

Diffuse infiltrative lymphocytosis syndrome (DILS) occurs in HIV-infected patients, characterized by marked bilateral parotid gland enlargement, sicca symptoms, generalized lymphadenopathy, and a striking circulating and tissue-infiltrating CD8+ hyperlymphocytosis with positive HLA-DR5/DR6 associations, in the absence of anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies.

Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) represents an exaggerated, hyperinflammatory response following antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation in patients with low CD4 counts, unmasking or paradoxically worsening occult opportunistic infections (tuberculosis, cryptococcosis, CMV) or preexisting autoimmune diseases.

Post-rituximab secondary hypogammaglobulinemia develops in up to 10% to 30% of patients receiving repeated B-cell depletion courses, especially those with baseline low-normal IgG or concomitant cyclophosphamide; persistent IgG levels below 400 mg/dL accompanied by recurrent sinopulmonary bacterial infections necessitate regular immunoglobulin replacement therapy.

Anatomic or functional asplenia markedly impairs clearance of unopsonized encapsulated bacteria and circulating Howell-Jolly bodies, predisposing to overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI) primarily caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae type b, demanding comprehensive vaccination and standby oral antibiotics.

Severe secondary hypogammaglobulinemia arises from non-immune protein-losing states including nephrotic syndrome and protein-losing enteropathy; selective urinary or gastrointestinal loss of lower molecular weight IgG occurs with relative preservation of IgM, retaining normal specific vaccine-induced antibody responses.

Good syndrome is the rare clinical association of thymoma with adult-onset hypogammaglobulinemia, combined with low or absent circulating CD19+ B cells, inverted CD4/CD8 T-cell ratios, and profound anergy, predisposing to severe opportunistic fungal (Candida, Pneumocystis), viral (CMV, HSV), and sinopulmonary bacterial infections.

Therapeutic immunosuppression with calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus) or mycophenolate mofetil impairs cell-mediated and humoral immune surveillance, mandating regular screening for BK polyomavirus nephropathy, cytomegalovirus reactivation, and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorders.

topics.title: Anaphylaxis, urticaria and hypersensitivity
mustKnow: The Gell and Coombs classification delineates four hypersensitivity mechanisms: Type I (IgE-mediated immediate mast cell degranulation, e.g., anaphylaxis), Type II (antibody-mediated cytotoxic, e.g., autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Goodpasture), Type III (immune complex deposition, e.g., SLE, serum sickness), and Type IV (cell-mediated delayed-type T-cell hypersensitivity, e.g., contact dermatitis, tuberculin test).

Anaphylaxis is an acute, life-threatening multisystem syndrome; immediate first-line management requires intramuscular adrenaline (epinephrine) injected into the anterolateral mid-thigh at a dose of 0.3 to 0.5 mg in adults (0.01 mg/kg in children) using a 1:1,000 (1 mg/mL) concentration, repeated every 5 to 15 minutes as needed.

Serum total tryptase rises transiently following systemic mast cell degranulation in anaphylaxis, peaking 1 to 2 hours after symptom onset and returning to baseline within 24 hours; a clinically meaningful acute rise is confirmed when peak tryptase exceeds 1.2 times baseline tryptase plus 2 ng/mL.

Chronic spontaneous urticaria is defined by pruritic wheals, angioedema, or both lasting for 6 weeks or longer without an identifiable trigger; refractory disease unyielding to quadrupled doses of second-generation non-sedating H1-antihistamines responds dramatically to omalizumab (monoclonal anti-IgE antibody) at 300 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks.

Hereditary angioedema (HAE) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by SERPING1 mutations leading to deficiency (Type I, 85%) or dysfunction (Type II, 15%) of C1 esterase inhibitor, resulting in excessive bradykinin generation; hallmarks include non-pruritic, non-pitting subepithelial swelling without urticaria, recurrent abdominal pain attacks, and laryngeal edema.

Laboratory screening for hereditary angioedema during quiescent or active phases reveals a persistently depressed serum C4 level (greater than 95% sensitivity), alongside decreased C1-INH antigenic protein in Type I and normal or elevated protein with impaired functional activity in Type II; C1q levels are characteristically normal in HAE but depressed in acquired C1-INH deficiency.

Acute attacks of hereditary angioedema fail to respond to adrenaline, antihistamines, or glucocorticoids; specific acute therapies target the contact-bradykinin pathway: plasma-derived or recombinant C1-INH concentrate, icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist), or ecallantide (plasma kallikrein inhibitor).

Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor-induced angioedema is caused by impaired enzymatic degradation of bradykinin and substance P; it accounts for up to 30% of angioedema presentations to emergency departments, can occur months or years after drug initiation, predominantly affects the tongue and pharynx, and mandates lifelong avoidance of ACE inhibitors and caution with ARBs.

topics.title: Mast cell and eosinophilic disorders
mustKnow: Systemic mastocytosis is characterized by clonal neoplastic proliferation of abnormal mast cells in bone marrow and extracutaneous organs; more than 90% to 95% of adult patients harbor the activating somatic point mutation KIT D816V in exon 17, which confers intrinsic resistance to imatinib.

Major diagnostic criterion for systemic mastocytosis is multifocal dense infiltrates of 15 or more mast cells in bone marrow or extracutaneous tissue; minor criteria include atypical spindle-shaped morphology, aberrant expression of CD25 and/or CD2 by mast cells, KIT D816V mutation, and baseline serum total tryptase persistently exceeding 20 ng/mL.

Hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) is defined by absolute blood eosinophil count exceeding 1,500/microL on two occasions at least 1 month apart, exclusion of secondary etiologies (parasitosis, drug allergy, vasculitis), and objective documentation of eosinophil-mediated organ damage (cardiac endomyocardial fibrosis, thromboembolism, neuropathy, pulmonary infiltrates).

The myeloproliferative variant of hypereosinophilic syndrome is driven by a cryptic interstitial deletion on chromosome 4q12 resulting in the constitutively active FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion tyrosine kinase; these patients have splenomegaly, elevated serum tryptase, cardiac involvement, and exhibit exquisite responsiveness to low-dose imatinib (100 mg daily).

Mepolizumab, a fully humanized IgG1 monoclonal antibody directed against IL-5 (the key cytokine regulating eosinophil survival, differentiation, and trafficking), is FDA/EMA-approved for patients with severe PDGFRA-negative hypereosinophilic syndrome and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA).

Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS syndrome) is a severe adverse drug reaction occurring 2 to 8 weeks after exposure (classically allopurinol, aromatic antiepileptics, sulfasalazine, vancomycin); characterized by extensive morbilliform eruption, facial edema, fever, marked eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytosis, internal organ involvement (hepatitis, nephritis), and human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) reactivation.

Eosinophilic fasciitis (Shulman disease) is characterized by painful symmetrical induration of the skin and subcutaneous tissues of the forearms and legs, sparing the digits, often following strenuous physical exercise; hallmarks include the 'groove sign' (linear depressions along superficial veins when the limb is elevated), peripheral eosinophilia, and deep en bloc full-thickness biopsy showing marked fascial thickening.

Avapritinib is an advanced selective KIT and PDGFRA activation-loop mutant kinase inhibitor approved for advanced systemic mastocytosis, demonstrating potent clinical responses and reduction in mast cell burden in patients with the refractory KIT D816V mutation.

topics.title: Rheumatoid arthritis pathogenesis and diagnosis
mustKnow: Genetic susceptibility to rheumatoid arthritis maps predominantly to the shared epitope, a conserved pentapeptide motif (QKRAA, QRRAA, or RRRAA) at positions 70 to 74 in the third hypervariable region of the HLA-DRB1 beta chain; gene-environment interaction with cigarette smoking dramatically multiplies the risk of developing anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA).

Peptidylarginine deiminase enzymes (PAD2 and PAD4), upregulated in inflamed airways and periodontitis (associated with Porphyromonas gingivalis), catalyze the calcium-dependent post-translational conversion of positively charged peptidylarginine into neutral citrulline, generating novel neoepitopes recognized by high-affinity ACPA.

The 2010 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for rheumatoid arthritis apply to patients with at least 1 joint with definite clinical synovitis not explained by another disease; a score of 6 or more out of 10 points classifies definite RA based on joint distribution (up to 5 points), serology (RF and ACPA, up to 3 points), symptom duration at least 6 weeks (1 point), and acute-phase reactants (1 point).

The rheumatoid synovial pannus is an invasive, hyperplastic, macrophage- and fibroblast-rich tissue that attaches to articular cartilage and bone; fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLS) secrete high levels of matrix metalloproteinases (MMP-1, MMP-3, MMP-13) and cathepsins that degrade type II collagen and aggrecan.

Osteoclastogenesis at the cartilage-pannus junction is driven by receptor activator of nuclear factor-kappa B ligand (RANKL), abundantly expressed by synovial T cells and activated FLS; binding to RANK on myeloid precursor cells stimulates osteoclast differentiation and drives subchondral marginal bone erosions.

Clinical hallmarks of early rheumatoid arthritis include symmetrical inflammatory polyarthritis predominantly involving the metacarpophalangeal (MCP), proximal interphalangeal (PIP), and metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joints, accompanied by prominent inflammatory morning stiffness lasting at least 30 to 60 minutes, with characteristic sparing of distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints and the thoracolumbar spine.

Advanced untreated rheumatoid arthritis produces characteristic tendon and joint deformities: ulnar deviation of the fingers at MCP joints, swan-neck deformity (hyperextension of PIP with flexion of DIP), boutonniere deformity (flexion of PIP with hyperextension of DIP), and hitchhiker thumb (Z-deformity).

Anti-carbamylated protein (anti-CarP) antibodies and anti-acetylated protein antibodies represent emerging post-translational modification autoantibodies in rheumatoid arthritis that identify severe erosive disease and poor radiographic outcomes, including in seronegative patients who lack RF and ACPA.

topics.title: Extra-articular rheumatoid arthritis
mustKnow: Rheumatoid nodules develop in 20% to 30% of patients with rheumatoid arthritis, virtually always in seropositive (RF and ACPA positive) individuals; histologically they demonstrate a central zone of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by a palisade of CD68+ epithelioid histiocytes and an outer rim of chronic mononuclear inflammatory cells, commonly over extensor pressure points.

Rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease (RA-ILD) occurs clinically in 10% of patients; unlike other connective tissue diseases where NSIP predominates, the most common HRCT and histological pattern in RA-ILD is usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) featuring subpleural basilar reticulation and honeycombing, which carries a poor prognosis.

Felty syndrome is the clinical triad of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, splenomegaly, and severe neutropenia (absolute neutrophil count <1,000 to 1,500/microL); it strongly associates with HLA-DR4 (*0401), high-titer RF, extra-articular disease, and refractory lower extremity cutaneous ulcers with recurrent bacterial infections.

Large granular lymphocyte (LGL) leukemia is closely linked with Felty syndrome, sharing severe neutropenia and splenomegaly; clonal expansion of CD3+ CD8+ CD57+ T cells with recurrent somatic activating mutations in STAT3 is identified in over 40% of cases, responding to immunosuppressive therapy with methotrexate or cyclophosphamide.

Rheumatoid vasculitis is a severe transmural necrotizing small- and medium-vessel arteritis complicating long-standing seropositive RA, manifesting with deep cutaneous ulcerations, digital gangrene, purpura, and mononeuritis multiplex; it carries high mortality and requires cyclophosphamide or rituximab combined with high-dose glucocorticoids.

Ocular manifestations of rheumatoid arthritis include secondary Sjogren keratoconjunctivitis sicca (most common), episcleritis, and deep necrotizing anterior scleritis; scleromalacia perforans represents severe painless anterior necrotizing scleritis without inflammation occurring in seropositive nodular RA that leads to globe rupture.

Cervical spine involvement in rheumatoid arthritis affects the synovial joints around the odontoid process, producing tenosynovitis of the transverse ligament and erosion of the dens; atlantoaxial subluxation is diagnosed on flexion lateral cervical radiographs when the anterior atlanto-dens interval (AADI) exceeds 3 mm (or >5 mm in severe instability), risking catastrophic spinal cord compression.

Persistent active high-grade systemic inflammation in rheumatoid arthritis drives AA (reactive) amyloidosis via sustained IL-6-mediated hepatic overproduction of serum amyloid A (SAA); deposition in glomeruli causes nephrotic syndrome and progressive renal failure, treatable by suppressive anti-IL-6 or anti-TNF biologics.

topics.title: Treat-to-target management of rheumatoid arthritis
mustKnow: The treat-to-target (T2T) strategy in rheumatoid arthritis mandates frequent objective disease activity assessment (every 1 to 3 months) aiming for stringent clinical remission (SDAI <=3.3, CDAI <=2.8, or Boolean 2.0 definition) or low disease activity, adjusting therapy within 3 to 6 months if target is not reached.

Methotrexate is the undisputed anchor conventional synthetic DMARD (csDMARD), initiated at 10 to 15 mg weekly and rapidly escalated to 20 to 25 mg weekly by mouth or subcutaneously with mandatory folic acid supplementation (5 mg weekly) to mitigate adverse effects without compromising efficacy.

Short-term glucocorticoid bridging (e.g., prednisone <=10 mg/day or equivalent) can be added when initiating or switching csDMARDs to achieve rapid symptomatic relief, but guidelines strictly recommend tapering and withdrawing glucocorticoids as rapidly as clinically feasible, ideally within 3 months.

If the treatment target is not achieved with initial csDMARD monotherapy and poor prognostic factors are present (high titers of RF or ACPA, high disease activity, early erosions), a biologic DMARD (TNF inhibitor, IL-6 receptor antagonist, or abatacept) or targeted synthetic DMARD (JAK inhibitor) should be added.

Triple csDMARD therapy comprising methotrexate, sulfasalazine (2 to 3 g daily), and hydroxychloroquine (200 to 400 mg daily) demonstrated non-inferiority to methotrexate plus etanercept in the landmark TEAR and RACAT trials, representing an efficacious, highly cost-effective strategy before biologics.

The ORAL Surveillance trial in patients with RA aged 50 or older with at least one cardiovascular risk factor showed higher incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and malignancy with tofacitinib compared to TNF inhibitors, prompting regulatory black-box warnings and positioning JAK inhibitors after bDMARD failure in high-risk patients.

Difficult-to-treat rheumatoid arthritis (D2T-RA), defined by EULAR, requires failure of at least two bDMARDs or tsDMARDs with different mechanisms of action after csDMARD failure, persistent signs of active or progressive disease, and clinician-patient management challenges, requiring multidisciplinary evaluation of non-adherence and comorbidities.

Once a patient achieves persistent clinical remission for at least 6 months, cautious dose reduction or interval extension of bDMARDs or tsDMARDs can be considered, whereas complete discontinuation carries a high relapse rate exceeding 50% and is generally discouraged while maintaining background csDMARD.

topics.title: Conventional synthetic DMARDs and toxicity
mustKnow: Methotrexate acts primarily via intracellular polyglutamylation and inhibition of aminoimidazolecarboxamide ribonucleotide (AICAR) transformylase, leading to extracellular accumulation of adenosine which exerts potent anti-inflammatory effects through A2A receptors on leukocytes.

Methotrexate-induced pneumonitis is an idiosyncratic non-dose-dependent hypersensitivity reaction occurring in 1% to 2% of patients; it presents with fever, non-productive cough, and dyspnea, showing bilateral ground-glass opacities with bronchoalveolar lavage lymphocytosis, mandating immediate drug discontinuation and systemic glucocorticoids.

Leflunomide is an isoxazole prodrug that is converted to active metabolite teriflunomide (A77 1726), which selectively inhibits dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH), blocking de novo pyrimidine synthesis in rapidly proliferating lymphocytes and causing G1 cell cycle arrest.

Due to extensive enterohepatic recirculation, leflunomide has a prolonged elimination half-life of 2 weeks and takes up to 2 years to clear completely; accelerated elimination washout using cholestyramine 8 g three times daily for 11 days (or activated charcoal 50 g 4 times daily) is mandatory prior to planned conception or in acute toxicity, ensuring plasma levels fall below 0.02 mg/L.

Sulfasalazine is cleaved by colonic azoreductase bacteria into 5-aminosalicylic acid and sulfapyridine, with sulfapyridine acting as the active moiety for peripheral arthritis; key adverse effects include dose-dependent nausea, reversible male infertility with oligospermia, agranulocytosis (most common in first 3 months), and hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

Hydroxychloroquine concentrates in acidic lysosomes, inhibiting antigen presentation, TLR7/TLR9 signaling, and matrix metalloproteinases; the American Academy of Ophthalmology recommends maintaining daily dosing at or below 5.0 mg/kg actual body weight to minimize long-term retinal toxicity, with baseline and annual spectral-domain OCT and visual field testing after 5 years.

Azathioprine is a prodrug of 6-mercaptopurine; patients with genetic deficiency of thiopurine S-methyltransferase (TPMT) or NUDT15 (especially prevalent in Asian populations) accumulate toxic 6-thioguanine nucleotides resulting in life-threatening pancytopenia, requiring genotyping or enzyme activity screening prior to therapy initiation.

Mycophenolate mofetil is a potent inhibitor of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH), selectively depleting guanosine nucleotides in lymphocytes; it carries severe embryofetal toxicity (microtia, cleft lip/palate, cardiac anomalies), demanding two forms of contraception and drug cessation at least 6 weeks before planned pregnancy.

topics.title: Biologic and targeted synthetic DMARDs
mustKnow: TNF inhibitors include monoclonal anti-TNF antibodies (infliximab [chimeric], adalimumab [human], golimumab [human]), pegylated Fab fragment (certolizumab pegol), and soluble p75 TNF receptor-Fc fusion protein (etanercept); certolizumab lacks an Fc portion and does not bind the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn), resulting in virtually zero placental transfer across trimesters.

Interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) or tuberculin skin test and chest radiography are mandatory before starting any biologic or targeted synthetic DMARD to detect latent tuberculosis; reactivation risk is substantially higher with monoclonal anti-TNF antibodies than with etanercept, requiring at least 1 month of prophylactic therapy before biologic initiation.

All patients scheduled for biologic or immunosuppressive therapy must be screened with HBsAg, anti-HBc, and anti-HBs; patients receiving B-cell depleting agents (rituximab) who are HBsAg-positive or anti-HBc-positive face catastrophic hepatitis B reactivation exceeding 40%, requiring antiviral prophylaxis with entecavir or tenofovir continued for at least 12 to 18 months post-depletion.

Tocilizumab and sarilumab are monoclonal antibodies targeting the IL-6 receptor (soluble and membrane-bound); because IL-6 is the principal driver of hepatic CRP synthesis, serum CRP drops to undetectable levels almost immediately regardless of intercurrent infection, rendering fever and CRP unreliable for diagnosing sepsis, and increasing vigilance for lower intestinal diverticular perforation.

Abatacept is a recombinant fusion protein consisting of the extracellular domain of cytotoxic T-lymphocyte antigen 4 (CTLA-4) linked to modified human IgG1 Fc; it selectively binds to CD80 and CD86 on antigen-presenting cells with higher affinity than CD28, blocking the co-stimulatory second signal required for T-cell activation.

Rituximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody targeting CD20 on pre-B and mature B lymphocytes (sparing pro-B cells and antibody-secreting plasma cells), administered as two 1,000 mg intravenous infusions 14 days apart with methylprednisolone premedication; efficacy is enhanced in seropositive (RF/ACPA-positive) RA, with peripheral B-cell depletion persisting for 6 to 9 months.

Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors are orally administered targeted small molecules: tofacitinib (preferential JAK1/JAK3), baricitinib (JAK1/JAK2), and upadacitinib (selective JAK1); they inhibit downstream STAT phosphorylation, effectively blocking signaling of multiple cytokines (IL-6, interferons, gamma-chain cytokines), with side effects including herpes zoster reactivation.

Biosimilars are biological medicinal products demonstrating bioequivalence, equivalent clinical efficacy, safety, and immunogenicity to an approved reference originator biologic without clinically meaningful differences, allowing extrapolation of indications across inflammatory diseases and driving substantial healthcare cost containment.

topics.title: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis
mustKnow: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is classified by the International League of Associations for Rheumatology (ILAR) criteria into seven categories based on clinical features in the first 6 months of disease in children younger than 16 years of age, with symptoms persisting for at least 6 weeks.

Oligoarticular JIA affects 4 or fewer joints during the first 6 months, predominantly large lower extremity joints (knee, ankle) in young girls; patients with positive antinuclear antibodies (ANA) face a 20% to 30% risk of asymptomatic, chronic, bilateral anterior uveitis that causes band keratopathy, cataracts, and blindness unless detected early by routine scheduled slit-lamp screening.

Systemic JIA (sJIA) is an autoinflammatory disorder characterized by daily quotidian spiking fevers, an evanescent salmon-pink maculopapular rash that surfaces with fever spikes, hepatosplenomegaly, generalized lymphadenopathy, polyserositis, and marked leukocytosis with extreme hyperferritinemia, driven by IL-1 and IL-6.

Macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) is a life-threatening complication in up to 10% of systemic JIA patients, classified under secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (sHLH); diagnostic hallmarks (2016 EULAR/ACR/PRINTO criteria) in a febrile patient with confirmed sJIA require serum ferritin >684 ng/mL plus two of: platelet count <=181,000/microL, AST >48 U/L, triglycerides >156 mg/dL, or fibrinogen <=360 mg/dL.

Therapy for systemic JIA with active systemic features prioritizes biological blockade of the IL-1 pathway (anakinra [recombinant IL-1 receptor antagonist], canakinumab [monoclonal anti-IL-1beta antibody]) or IL-6 pathway (tocilizumab), frequently enabling rapid glucocorticoid withdrawal.

Enthesitis-related arthritis (ERA) occurs predominantly in boys older than 6 years, linked to HLA-B27, presenting with lower extremity asymmetric arthritis and tender enthesitis (Achilles tendon insertion, plantar fascia, patellar tendon), acute symptomatic unilateral anterior uveitis, and potential progression to axial spondyloarthritis.

Polyarticular JIA involves 5 or more joints during the first 6 months: RF-negative polyarticular JIA is heterogeneous, while RF-positive polyarticular JIA resembles adult rheumatoid arthritis, occurs in adolescent girls with shared epitope HLA-DRB1 alleles, and exhibits an aggressive erosive, disabling clinical course.

Active macrophage activation syndrome demands emergency treatment with high-dose intravenous pulse methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg/day up to 1 g/day for 3 days) combined with high-dose anakinra (up to 8 to 10 mg/kg/day) or cyclosporine; refractory cases require etoposide or emapalumab (monoclonal anti-IFN-gamma antibody).

topics.title: Adult onset Still disease
mustKnow: Adult-onset Still disease (AOSD) is a severe systemic autoinflammatory disorder of young adults; the Yamaguchi criteria require at least 5 features with at least 2 major criteria (fever >=39C lasting >=1 week, arthralgia/arthritis >=2 weeks, typical salmon-pink evanescent non-pruritic maculopapular rash, and leukocytosis >=10,000/microL with >=80% granulocytes).

Minor Yamaguchi criteria for adult-onset Still disease include sore throat (non-suppurative pharyngitis, often the herald symptom), lymphadenopathy and/or splenomegaly, hepatic dysfunction (elevated AST, ALT, LDH), and negative testing for antinuclear antibodies and rheumatoid factor.

Serum ferritin is massively elevated in adult-onset Still disease, often 5-fold to 20-fold above upper normal limit (frequently exceeding 3,000 to 5,000 ng/mL); a depressed glycosylated ferritin fraction <=20% (normal >50%) has high diagnostic specificity of 80% to 90% for AOSD in a febrile patient.

Fever in adult-onset Still disease classically follows a daily quotidian or double quotidian pattern with rapid temperature spikes exceeding 39 degrees Celsius characteristically in the late afternoon or early evening, returning to baseline without antipyretics, during which the fleeting salmon-pink rash becomes prominent.

Articular involvement in AOSD can evolve into a distinctive, progressive, non-erosive intercarpal and carpometacarpal ankylosis with preservation of joint spaces at the MCP and PIP joints, producing an isolated pericapitate or pancarpal ankylosis on wrist radiography.

Initial therapy for moderate-to-severe adult-onset Still disease relies on systemic glucocorticoids (prednisone 0.5 to 1 mg/kg/day); however, steroid dependency or refractoriness occurs in over 40% to 60% of patients, requiring early initiation of steroid-sparing agents.

Biological agents targeting IL-1 (anakinra, canakinumab) demonstrate remarkable efficacy, particularly for systemic features (fever, rash, hyperferritinemia) and in preventing macrophage activation syndrome; the IL-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab is equally potent, especially for patients with persistent polyarticular manifestations.

Macrophage activation syndrome is the most devastating acute complication of adult-onset Still disease, manifesting with paradoxical sudden drop in ESR (due to consumptive hypofibrinogenemia), dropping platelet counts, extreme hyperferritinemia, coagulopathy, and neurological dysfunction, requiring immediate high-dose pulse methylprednisolone and IL-1 blockade.

topics.title: Axial spondyloarthritis and ankylosing spondylitis
mustKnow: Axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) is strongly linked to HLA-B27 (present in 85% to 90% of ankylosing spondylitis in Caucasian populations); primary pathogenic hypotheses include presentation of arthritogenic self-peptides, intracellular HLA-B27 heavy chain misfolding inducing ER stress and IL-23 activation, and cell-surface HLA-B27 free heavy-chain homodimer formation triggering killer cell immunoglobulin-like receptors (KIRs).

Inflammatory back pain (IBP) per ASAS consensus criteria requires at least 4 of 5 parameters: age of onset <40 years, insidious onset, improvement with exercise, no improvement with rest, and pain at night (with improvement upon getting up); morning stiffness typically exceeds 30 to 45 minutes.

The ASAS classification criteria for axial SpA apply to patients with back pain >=3 months and age of onset <45 years; entry occurs via either the imaging arm (sacroiliitis on imaging [definite active MRI sacroiliitis or radiographic sacroiliitis by modified New York criteria] plus >=1 SpA feature) or the clinical arm (HLA-B27 positive plus >=2 other SpA features).

Non-radiographic axial SpA (nr-axSpA) is distinguished from radiographic ankylosing spondylitis by the absence of bilateral grade >=2 or unilateral grade >=3 sacroiliitis on plain radiographs; MRI of sacroiliac joints reveals active subchondral bone marrow edema on STIR sequences with comparable symptom burden and therapeutic responsiveness.

Clinical spinal assessment tools measure disease progression and functional impairment: Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index (BASDAI), Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Score (ASDAS, incorporating CRP), modified Schober test (<5 cm expansion indicating restricted lumbar flexion), chest expansion (<2.5 cm measured at 4th intercostal space), and occiput-to-wall distance.

Continuous treatment with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) at maximum tolerated anti-inflammatory doses is recommended as first-line pharmacological therapy for active symptomatic axial SpA, providing rapid symptomatic relief and potentially attenuating structural radiographic progression.

Conventional synthetic DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, leflunomide) are ineffective for purely axial disease; patients with persistently active axSpA despite at least two different NSAIDs used over 4 weeks qualify for a biologic DMARD: TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept, golimumab, certolizumab) or IL-17A inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab) or IL-17A/F dual inhibitor (bimekizumab).

Extra-skeletal manifestations of ankylosing spondylitis include acute unilateral anterior uveitis (25% to 30%, responsive to topical glucocorticoids), subclinical or clinical inflammatory bowel disease, ascending aortitis with aortic root dilatation and aortic regurgitation, cardiac conduction blocks, and apical pulmonary fibrocystic disease colonized by Aspergillus.

topics.title: Management of spondyloarthritis
mustKnow: Continuous treatment with oral NSAIDs at maximum anti-inflammatory doses is recommended as first-line pharmacological therapy for symptomatic active axial spondyloarthritis, providing rapid symptomatic relief and reducing inflammatory spinal stiffness.

Conventional synthetic DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, leflunomide) have proven lack of efficacy for purely axial inflammatory disease and are not recommended for isolated sacroiliitis or spondylitis.
Sulfasalazine (2 to 3 g daily) is conditionally recommended only for patients with prominent peripheral arthritis or concomitant inflammatory bowel disease associated with axial spondyloarthritis.

Patients with persistently active axial SpA (ASDAS >=2.1 or BASDAI >=4) despite trials of at least two different NSAIDs over 4 weeks qualify for escalation to a biologic DMARD or targeted synthetic DMARD.

First-line biologic choices include TNF inhibitors (monoclonal antibodies: infliximab, adalimumab, golimumab, certolizumab; or soluble receptor: etanercept) and IL-17A inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab), both demonstrating equivalent clinical efficacy.

In patients with concomitant recurrent anterior uveitis or active inflammatory bowel disease, monoclonal anti-TNF antibodies (infliximab, adalimumab, certolizumab) are strongly preferred over etanercept or IL-17 inhibitors.
Bimekizumab, a dual monoclonal antibody neutralizing both IL-17A and IL-17F, and oral JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, upadacitinib) are approved options for active axial SpA failing TNF inhibitors.

Structured regular physical therapy and home-based spinal extension exercises are essential non-pharmacological pillars to preserve spinal mobility, maintain thoracic chest expansion, and prevent spinal kyphotic deformity.

topics.title: Psoriatic arthritis
mustKnow: Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) occurs in up to 30% of patients with cutaneous psoriasis, typically developing 5 to 10 years after skin lesions, although arthritis precedes psoriasis in 15% of cases; nail dystrophy (pitting, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis, oil-drop sign) strongly correlates with enthesitis of the distal phalanx extensor tendon insertion and DIP joint arthritis.

The CASPAR (Classification Criteria for Psoriatic Arthritis) criteria require established inflammatory articular disease (joint, spine, or entheseal) plus at least 3 points from five categories: current psoriasis (2 points) or personal/family history (1 point), typical psoriatic nail dystrophy (1 point), negative rheumatoid factor (1 point), current or historical dactylitis (1 point), and radiographic evidence of juxta-articular new bone formation (1 point).

Moll and Wright recognized five clinical patterns of psoriatic arthritis: asymmetric oligoarthritis (most common initially), symmetric polyarthritis (resembling RA but RF-negative), distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint predominant arthritis, axial spondyloarthritis/sacroiliitis, and arthritis mutilans with severe digital telescoping ('opera-glass hand').

Dactylitis ('sausage digit') represents diffuse, uniform, painful swelling of an entire finger or toe caused by concurrent flexor tenosynovitis and adjacent soft tissue enthesitis, serving as a hallmark diagnostic and poor prognostic indicator in psoriatic arthritis.

Radiographic hallmarks of psoriatic arthritis reflect a unique coexistence of destructive erosive bone changes and proliferative periosteal new bone formation in the same joint: marginal erosions with adjacent bone whittling, pencil-in-cup deformity, periostitis ('whiskering'), acro-osteolysis of distal phalanges, and asymmetric paraspinal coarse syndesmophytes.

In peripheral psoriatic arthritis, methotrexate is the most common first-line conventional synthetic DMARD due to dual cutaneous and joint efficacy; leflunomide and sulfasalazine represent alternatives, while systemic glucocorticoids are used with extreme caution because rapid steroid taper can precipitate life-threatening generalized pustular psoriasis (von Zumbusch).

Biologic and targeted synthetic therapies for psoriatic arthritis span multiple validated cytokine pathways: TNF inhibitors, IL-17A inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab), IL-17A/F dual inhibitor (bimekizumab), IL-12/23 inhibitor (ustekinumab), IL-23p19 specific inhibitors (guselkumab, risankizumab), oral phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE4) inhibitor (apremilast), and JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, upadacitinib).

Deucravacitinib is an oral, first-in-class selective allosteric TYK2 (tyrosine kinase 2) inhibitor that binds to the regulatory pseudokinase domain rather than the conserved ATP-catalytic site, providing selective inhibition of IL-23, IL-12, and type I interferon signaling without off-target JAK1/2/3 hematologic or thrombotic toxicities, approved for plaque psoriasis and active in PsA.

topics.title: Reactive arthritis
mustKnow: Reactive arthritis is an acute, sterile inflammatory synovitis developing 1 to 4 weeks following a distant gastrointestinal or urogenital infection; classic enteric triggers include Salmonella enterica, Shigella flexneri, Yersinia enterocolitica, and Campylobacter jejuni, whereas the predominant venereal trigger is Chlamydia trachomatis.

Genetic susceptibility is strongly driven by HLA-B27, present in 60% to 85% of patients with reactive arthritis, predisposing to greater clinical severity, frequent axial involvement, chronic recurrent relapses, and widespread mucocutaneous extra-articular manifestations.

The classical clinical triad (historically termed Reiter syndrome) comprises non-gonococcal urethritis or cervicitis, conjunctivitis, and acute asymmetric inflammatory oligoarthritis predominantly involving large weight-bearing joints of the lower extremities (knees, ankles, subtalar joints).

Dermatological hallmarks of reactive arthritis include keratoderma blennorrhagicum (hyperkeratotic, pustular papules on the palms and soles resembling pustular psoriasis) and circinate balanitis (painless superficial serpiginous erosions on the glans penis and coronal sulcus).

Oral lesions in reactive arthritis consist of small, shallow, painless mucosal ulcers on the tongue, hard palate, and buccal mucosa, which frequently go unnoticed by the patient unless actively inspected during the clinical examination.

First-line therapy for acute reactive arthritis centers on full-dose NSAIDs; intra-articular glucocorticoid injections are highly effective for refractory mono- or oligoarthritis, while systemic glucocorticoids are reserved for patients with severe polyarticular flares or refractory systemic inflammation.

When Chlamydia trachomatis urogenital infection is confirmed by first-void urine or cervical swab nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT), antimicrobial therapy with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days or single-dose azithromycin 1 g is mandatory for the patient and all sexual partners, although antibiotics do not alter the course of post-dysenteric enteric reactive arthritis.

Patients who fail to achieve remission within 3 to 6 months develop chronic reactive arthritis (affecting 15% to 20%); sulfasalazine (2 to 3 g daily) is the csDMARD of choice for chronic peripheral arthritis, with refractory cases responding to anti-TNF biologics.

topics.title: Enteropathic arthritis
mustKnow: Enteropathic arthritis encompasses inflammatory musculoskeletal manifestations associated with Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis, affecting 15% to 20% of IBD patients.

Orchard Type 1 peripheral arthritis is an acute, asymmetric, pauciarticular (<5 joints) arthritis involving knees and ankles; attacks are self-limiting (<10 weeks) and parallel mucosal gut inflammation, resolving with bowel treatment.

Orchard Type 2 peripheral arthritis is a symmetric polyarthritis (>=5 joints) involving small joints (MCP, PIP, wrists) that runs an indolent, persistent course lasting months to years completely independent of active bowel inflammation.

Axial involvement occurs in 5% to 10% of IBD patients, with sacroiliitis and progressive spondylitis that progress independently of gut activity; HLA-B27 is positive in 50% to 60%, compared to 90% in idiopathic ankylosing spondylitis.
Oral NSAIDs must be used with extreme caution or avoided in enteropathic arthritis due to the established risk of triggering exacerbations or flares of underlying gastrointestinal mucosal ulceration.

Sulfasalazine (2 to 3 g daily) is the preferred csDMARD for mild-to-moderate colonic IBD and concomitant Type 1 peripheral arthritis, while oral or parenteral methotrexate is effective for luminal Crohn disease and peripheral synovitis.

Monoclonal anti-TNF antibodies (infliximab, adalimumab, certolizumab pegol) effectively treat both active luminal bowel inflammation and axial/peripheral enteropathic arthritis; etanercept is ineffective and contraindicated as it does not heal mucosal Crohn disease.

IL-17A inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab) are strictly contraindicated in enteropathic arthritis and IBD because IL-17 maintains mucosal gut barrier integrity, and trials demonstrate clear risk of inducing de novo Crohn disease or severe exacerbations.

topics.title: Gout and hyperuricemia
mustKnow: Hyperuricemia exceeds the physiological solubility limit of monosodium urate of 6.8 mg/dL (404 micromol/L) at 37 degrees Celsius; renal underexcretion via URAT1 and GLUT9 accounts for >90% of primary cases.
Acute gout presents with rapid-onset, excruciating inflammatory monoarthritis peaking within 12 to 24 hours, involving the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra) in over 50% of initial attacks.

Synovial fluid analysis under compensated polarized light microscopy demonstrates intracellular, needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals displaying strong negative birefringence (yellow parallel to the compensator axis).

First-line therapy for acute gout flares includes low-dose colchicine (1.2 mg immediately followed by 0.6 mg 1 hour later), oral NSAIDs, or systemic glucocorticoids (prednisone 30 to 35 mg daily for 5 days).

Urate-lowering therapy (ULT) is indicated for patients with >=1 subcutaneous tophi, radiographic damage from gout, or frequent flares (>=2 per year), initiated during an acute flare alongside anti-inflammatory prophylaxis.

Allopurinol is the preferred first-line xanthine oxidase inhibitor for all patients, starting at <=100 mg daily (lower in CKD) and titrated every 2 to 5 weeks to achieve a serum urate target strictly <6.0 mg/dL (<5.0 mg/dL in severe tophaceous gout).

Screening for HLA-B*5801 is strongly recommended before starting allopurinol in patients of Southeast Asian and African descent due to a high risk of allopurinol severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCAR, SJS/TEN).

Anti-inflammatory flare prophylaxis with low-dose colchicine (0.5 to 0.6 mg daily) or low-dose NSAIDs is mandatory when initiating urate-lowering therapy, continued for at least 3 to 6 months after achieving target urate.

topics.title: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease
mustKnow: Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystal deposition disease is driven by increased extracellular concentrations of inorganic pyrophosphate (PPi) generated by ectonucleotide pyrophosphatase/phosphodiesterase 1 (ENPP1) and transported out of chondrocytes via the ANKH transmembrane transporter.

Chondrocalcinosis is the radiographic hallmark of CPPD, manifesting as fine linear or punctate calcific radiodensities within fibrocartilage (knee menisci, triangular fibrocartilage of wrist, symphysis pubis) and hyaline articular cartilage.

The 2023 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for CPPD disease require microscopic verification of positively birefringent rhomboid crystals or bilateral chondrocalcinosis on imaging, establishing standardized criteria across clinical phenotypes.

Acute calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis (pseudogout) presents as acute, intensely painful mono- or oligoarthritis, most commonly affecting the knee (in >50% of cases), wrist, or shoulder, frequently provoked by acute medical illness, surgery (parathyroidectomy, joint arthroplasty), or intra-articular hyaluronan.

Chronic CPPD inflammatory arthritis (pseudo-rheumatoid pattern) manifests as symmetrical polyarthritis involving wrists, MCP joints, and elbows, often with subchondral cyst formation and morning stiffness, but negative for RF and ACPA.

Crowned dens syndrome results from CPPD crystal deposition in the cruciform and transverse ligaments around the odontoid process, presenting in elderly patients with severe neck pain, marked cervical stiffness, fever, and elevated inflammatory markers, diagnosed by retro-odontoid calcification on non-contrast cervical CT.

Metabolic and endocrine disorders strongly predisposing to early-onset or extensive CPPD include hereditary hemochromatosis (HFE mutations, iron overload inhibiting pyrophosphatase), primary hyperparathyroidism, hypomagnesemia (Gitelman syndrome), and hypophosphatasia (ALPL mutations).

Therapy for acute CPPD attacks parallels gout: intra-articular glucocorticoid aspiration and injection, oral NSAIDs, or low-dose colchicine; for frequent recurrent pseudogout flares, daily low-dose colchicine (0.5 to 0.6 mg daily) provides effective long-term flare prophylaxis.

topics.title: Osteoarthritis
mustKnow: Osteoarthritis is a disorder of the whole synovial joint organ, featuring progressive cartilage breakdown, subchondral bone sclerosis, osteophyte formation, and low-grade synovitis driven by biomechanical and inflammatory stress.

Chondrocytes undergo phenotypic transition under mechanical stress, expressing RUNX2 and secreting matrix metalloproteinases (MMP-13) and aggrecanases (ADAMTS-4 and ADAMTS-5) that degrade type II collagen and aggrecan.

Radiographic severity is scored from grade 0 to 4 using the Kellgren-Lawrence scale: grade 2 demonstrates definite osteophytes with possible joint space narrowing, and grade 4 exhibits severe sclerosis, marked joint space obliteration, and bone deformity.

Nodal hand osteoarthritis is characterized by bony enlargements: Heberden nodes at distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints and Bouchard nodes at proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints, with frequent base-of-thumb first carpometacarpal joint involvement.

Erosive hand osteoarthritis affects postmenopausal women, featuring acute inflammatory episodes with central subchondral cortical bone erosions producing the classical 'gull-wing' appearance on plain radiography.

Non-pharmacological core therapy is fundamental for all patients: structured land-based or aquatic exercise programs, biomechanical education, and weight loss (>=5% to 10% weight reduction significantly relieves joint loading and pain).

Topical NSAIDs (e.g., topical diclofenac) are strongly recommended as first-line pharmacological treatment for knee osteoarthritis before initiating oral NSAIDs, providing equivalent local pain relief with superior systemic safety.

Duloxetine is recommended for knee or generalized osteoarthritis with centralized pain or concomitant depression; oral glucosamine, chondroitin, and hyaluronic acid injections are conditionally or strongly recommended against due to lack of proven benefit over placebo.

topics.title: Osteoporosis and metabolic bone disease
mustKnow: Osteoporosis is defined by the World Health Organization as a bone mineral density (BMD) T-score of -2.5 or lower at the lumbar spine, femoral neck, or total hip on dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), or the presence of a low-trauma fragility fracture of the hip or vertebra regardless of BMD.

Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis (GIOP) is the most frequent secondary cause of osteoporosis; bone loss occurs rapidly within the first 3 to 6 months of glucocorticoid therapy (prednisone >=2.5 to 5 mg/day) primarily through increased osteoclast survival and profound suppression of osteoblast function and osteocalcin synthesis.

The FRAX tool calculates the 10-year probability of a major osteoporotic fracture and hip fracture; the FRAX glucocorticoid adjustment increases fracture risk by approximately 15% to 20% for prednisone doses >7.5 mg daily.

Oral bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate) and intravenous zoledronic acid (5 mg annually) inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP) synthase in the mevalonate pathway, inducing osteoclast apoptosis and reducing vertebral and non-vertebral fracture rates; rare adverse events include atypical subtrochanteric femoral fractures and osteonecrosis of the jaw (ONJ).

Denosumab is a fully human IgG2 monoclonal antibody that binds with high affinity to RANKL, preventing osteoclast formation and bone resorption; abrupt discontinuation triggers a rebound surge in osteoclastogenesis and rapid bone loss, with high risk of multiple rebound vertebral fractures unless immediately followed by bisphosphonate consolidation.

Anabolic osteoanabolic agents are prioritized for very high fracture risk or severe GIOP: teriparatide (recombinant human PTH 1-34) and abaloparatide (PTHrP analog) stimulate osteoblastic bone formation when administered intermittently daily, whereas romosozumab is a dual-action sclerostin inhibitor that simultaneously increases bone formation and decreases resorption.

Osteomalacia in adults results from defective bone matrix mineralization due to severe vitamin D deficiency, renal phosphate wasting (oncogenic osteomalacia mediated by FGF23), or hypophosphatasia; hallmarks include widespread bone pain, proximal muscle weakness, waddling gait, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and pseudofractures (Looser zones) on plain radiographs.

Paget disease of bone (osteitis deformans) is a focal disorder of accelerated, disorganized bone remodeling driven by hyperactive osteoclasts linked to SQSTM1 (p62) mutations; manifestations include localized bone pain, skeletal deformity (sabre shin, skull enlargement causing leontiasis ossea), hearing loss from cranial nerve compression, markedy elevated serum alkaline phosphatase, and a risk of secondary osteosarcoma in <1%.

topics.title: Arthropathy of systemic and endocrine disease
mustKnow: Hereditary hemochromatosis arthropathy affects 40% to 60% of patients carrying homozygous C282Y HFE mutations; it presents with non-inflammatory degenerative changes in the second and third metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints with hook-like osteophytes and chondrocalcinosis.

Ochronotic arthropathy (alkaptonuria) is an autosomal recessive inborn error of tyrosine metabolism caused by homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase (HGD) deficiency, leading to accumulation of homogentisic acid which binds collagen and turns connective tissues dark blue-black.

Spinal radiographs in ochronosis demonstrate characteristic universal wafer-like intervertebral disc calcifications with profound disc space narrowing across multiple lumbar levels, alongside secondary osteopenia and brittle joint cartilage.

Acromegalic arthropathy results from chronic excess of growth hormone and IGF-1, causing accelerated cartilage hypertrophy, widening of joint spaces initially followed by premature secondary osteoarthritic degradation, and carpal tunnel syndrome in over 50%.

Thyroid acropachy is a rare manifestation of autoimmune thyroid disease (predominantly Graves disease with high-titer TSH receptor antibodies), presenting with the triad of digital clubbing, soft tissue swelling of digits, and asymptomatic subperiosteal new bone formation in the tubular bones of hands and feet.

Neuropathic arthropathy (Charcot joint) results from loss of pain sensation and proprioception: classic etiologies include diabetic peripheral sensory neuropathy (affecting tarsal and metatarsophalangeal joints) and tabes dorsalis or syringomyelia (affecting upper extremity shoulder and elbow joints).

Radiographic stages of Charcot joint progress from acute fragmentation and capsular distension to massive osteolysis, joint dislocation, and exuberant disorganized periosteal new bone formation ('bag of bones' appearance).

Management of Charcot foot requires immediate, strict non-weight-bearing immobilization with total contact casting (TCC) during the acute active inflammatory stage, followed by customized orthotic bracing (Charcot restraint orthotic walker [CROW]) to prevent catastrophic foot collapse.

topics.title: Osteonecrosis and other bone disorders
mustKnow: Osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis, aseptic necrosis) results from compromised microvascular blood supply to bone, leading to osteocyte death, subchondral microfractures, and eventual articular surface collapse.

The femoral head is the most frequent anatomical site (bilateral in over 70% of non-traumatic cases); major systemic etiologies include systemic glucocorticoid therapy, heavy alcohol consumption, sickle cell disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, and decompression sickness.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the gold standard diagnostic modality in early pre-radiographic stages, displaying a focal subchondral serpiginous band of low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and the pathognomonic 'double line sign' on T2-weighted images.

The Ficat-Arlet and Steinberg radiographic staging systems classify femoral head osteonecrosis from stage 0 (normal radiograph and MRI) to stage IV/VI (subchondral collapse, crescent sign, joint space loss, and secondary osteoarthritis).

The 'crescent sign' on plain radiographs represents a linear subchondral lucency indicating structural microfracture and detachment of necrotic trabeculae from overlying intact articular cartilage, predicting imminent mechanical collapse.

In pre-collapse stages (Ficat I and II), joint-preserving surgical interventions such as core decompression (with or without bone marrow aspirate concentrate [BMAC]) decrease elevated intraosseous pressure, stimulate angiogenesis, and delay disease progression.

Once structural femoral head collapse or crescent sign has developed (Ficat III and IV), core decompression is ineffective, and total hip arthroplasty (THA) is the definitive surgical management of choice.

Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ) is a distinct entity defined by exposed necrotic bone in the maxillofacial region persisting >8 weeks in patients exposed to antiresorptive agents (zoledronic acid, denosumab) or antiangiogenic drugs without prior radiation therapy.

topics.title: SLE pathogenesis and classification
mustKnow: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a prototypic multiorgan autoimmune disease characterized by defective clearance of apoptotic cell debris, leading to secondary necrosis and exposure of intracellular nuclear autoantigens (chromatin, snRNPs, DNA) to the immune system.

Endosomal Toll-like receptors (TLR7 and TLR9) in plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) recognize internalized RNA- and DNA-containing immune complexes via Fc-gamma-RIIa (CD32), driving continuous, massive production of type I interferons (IFN-alpha and IFN-beta), establishing the characteristic pathogenic 'interferon gene signature'.

B-cell hyperreactivity and breach of central and peripheral tolerance in SLE are driven by excess B-cell activating factor (BAFF, also known as BLyS) and a proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL), promoting the survival, expansion, and maturation of autoreactive plasma cells producing high-affinity pathogenic autoantibodies.

Genetic susceptibility to SLE includes homozygous loss-of-function mutations in early classical complement components (C1q, C1r, C1s, C4A/B), where C1q deficiency confers a >90% penetrance of early-onset, severe cutaneous and neuropsychiatric lupus.

Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) generated during exaggerated NETosis expose citrullinated histones, LL-37, and modified double-stranded DNA; impaired NET degradation by serum DNase I promotes persistent immune complex formation and induces endothelial injury in lupus nephritis.

Immune complex deposition in tissues activates the classical complement cascade, generating anaphylatoxins (C3a and C5a) that recruit neutrophils, monocytes, and mac-1 expressing inflammatory cells, producing tissue damage and hypocomplementemia (depressed C3 and C4) during active disease flares.

T-cell abnormalities in SLE include defective IL-2 production, altered T-cell receptor (TCR) zeta chain signaling (replaced by Fc-epsilon-RI-gamma), hyperactive calcium signaling, and impaired suppression by CD4+ CD25+ FOXP3+ regulatory T cells, promoting follicular helper T (Tfh) cell support of autoantibody synthesis.

Environmental triggers of lupus flares include ultraviolet (UV) radiation (inducing keratinocyte apoptosis and translocation of Ro/SSA and nuclear antigens to the cell surface), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection with molecular mimicry between EBNA-1 and Sm antigens, and sex hormones (estrogen promoting B-cell survival).

topics.title: Organ manifestations of SLE
mustKnow: Cardiac involvement in systemic lupus erythematosus affects pericardium, myocardium, endocardium, and coronary arteries; pericarditis is the most common cardiac manifestation (in 25% to 50%), typically presenting with positional pleuritic chest pain and friction rub.

Libman-Sacks endocarditis (verrucous non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis) is characterized by sterile fibrovascular vegetations on mitral and aortic valves, strongly linked to antiphospholipid antibodies and conferring high risk of cardioembolic stroke and secondary bacterial endocarditis.

Accelerated atherosclerosis in SLE confers a 5- to 10-fold increased risk of coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction, escalating to >50-fold in young premenopausal women with lupus due to chronic systemic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and glucocorticoid therapy.

Pulmonary manifestations include acute lupus pneumonitis, diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH, an emergency presenting with hemoptysis and falling hematocrit), pleuritis with exudative pleural effusions, and chronic fibrosing interstitial lung disease.

Shrinking lung syndrome is a rare manifestation characterized by unexplained progressive dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, elevation of hemidiaphragms on chest imaging, and restrictive ventilatory defect with proportional reductions in lung volumes without parenchymal interstitial lung disease.

Gastrointestinal involvement includes lupus mesenteric vasculitis (lupus enteritis), presenting with severe acute abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting; abdominal CT shows characteristic bowel wall thickening, target sign, and engorgement of mesenteric vessels ('comb sign').

Hematologic manifestations include autoimmune hemolytic anemia (warm IgG Coombs-positive), immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), and severe leukopenia/lymphopenia, with lymphopenia (<1,000/microL) correlating closely with active systemic disease flares.

Ophthalmic manifestations include dry eye keratoconjunctivitis sicca, episcleritis, and retinal vasculitis (lupus retinopathy) characterized by cotton-wool spots (cytoid bodies) and retinal hemorrhages, reflecting active cerebral or systemic microvascular disease.

topics.title: Lupus nephritis
mustKnow: Lupus nephritis affects 40% to 60% of SLE patients; renal biopsy is mandatory for any patient with unexplained persistent proteinuria >=0.5 g/24 hours (or spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio >=0.5 mg/mg) or active urinary sediment with dysmorphic hematuria or cellular casts.

The ISN/RPS 2003 (updated 2018) histological classification stratifies lupus nephritis into six classes: Class I (minimal mesangial), Class II (mesangial proliferative), Class III (focal proliferative, involving <50% of glomeruli), Class IV (diffuse proliferative, involving >=50% of glomeruli), Class V (membranous), and Class VI (advanced sclerosing, >=90% globally sclerosed glomeruli).

Immunofluorescence microscopy of lupus nephritis characteristically reveals the 'full-house' pattern: dense granular deposition of IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, and C1q in mesangium and capillary loops, accompanied by prominent subendothelial immune complex deposits (wire-loop lesions) in active Class IV disease.

First-line induction therapy for active Class III and IV proliferative lupus nephritis combines glucocorticoids with either mycophenolate mofetil (MMF, target dose 2 to 3 g daily) or low-dose intravenous cyclophosphamide (Euro-Lupus regimen: 500 mg every 2 weeks for 6 doses, total 3 g), both demonstrating equivalent renal remission rates.

Triple immunosuppressive therapy ('multitarget therapy') combining mycophenolate mofetil, a calcineurin inhibitor (tacrolimus 2 to 4 mg daily or voclosporin), and low-dose glucocorticoids produces significantly higher and faster complete renal response rates in proliferative and mixed Class III/IV plus V lupus nephritis.

Belimumab, a recombinant human monoclonal antibody against soluble BAFF (BLyS), is FDA/EMA-approved for active lupus nephritis based on the BLISS-LN trial; when added to standard-of-care induction (MMF or Euro-Lupus), belimumab significantly improves Primary Efficacy Renal Response and reduces renal flares.

Maintenance therapy for lupus nephritis follows successful induction: mycophenolate mofetil (1 to 2 g daily) or azathioprine (2 mg/kg daily) is continued for at least 3 to 5 years before considering very gradual, cautious drug withdrawal, alongside indefinite background hydroxychloroquine.

Background supportive care is mandatory in all lupus nephritis patients: hydroxychloroquine (up to 5 mg/kg actual body weight) reduces renal flares, protects against thrombotic events, and improves survival; ACE inhibitors or ARBs target proteinuria reduction and strict blood pressure control (<120 mmHg systolic per KDIGO 2024).

topics.title: Management of SLE
mustKnow: Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is strongly recommended for all patients with SLE unless contraindicated, maintaining daily dosing at or below 5.0 mg/kg actual body weight to minimize long-term retinal toxicity, halving overall mortality and preventing disease flares.

The therapeutic goal in SLE is achieving the Lupus Low Disease Activity State (LLDAS) or clinical remission: LLDAS requires SLEDAI-2K <=4, no new organ activity, physician global assessment <=1.0, and maintenance prednisone <=7.5 mg daily.

Systemic glucocorticoids should be rapidly tapered aiming for a maintenance dose of prednisone <=5.0 mg/day or complete withdrawal whenever clinically feasible, to prevent irreversible cardiovascular, cataract, and osteoporotic organ damage accrual.

Methotrexate (15 to 25 mg weekly) or azathioprine (2 mg/kg daily) is recommended as early steroid-sparing therapy for active musculoskeletal and cutaneous manifestations failing hydroxychloroquine monotherapy.

Mycophenolate mofetil (2 to 3 g daily) is the preferred immunosuppressive agent for renal and severe extra-articular manifestations, while being strictly contraindicated during pregnancy due to embryofetal teratogenicity.

Belimumab (anti-BAFF/BLyS monoclonal antibody, 10 mg/kg IV monthly or 200 mg SC weekly) is indicated for active SLE failing first-line csDMARDs and in active lupus nephritis, significantly reducing flares and glucocorticoid requirements.

Anifrolumab (anti-IFNAR1 monoclonal antibody, 300 mg IV every 4 weeks) is recommended for moderate-to-severe SLE with refractory cutaneous or musculoskeletal activity, with herpes zoster vaccination prioritized before initiation.

Rituximab (anti-CD20) is recommended off-label for severe, refractory, organ-threatening disease manifestations (severe thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, refractory proliferative lupus nephritis, or refractory CNS lupus) failing standard therapies.

topics.title: Drug-induced and cutaneous lupus
mustKnow: Drug-induced lupus erythematosus (DILE) is an idiosyncratic autoimmune reaction developing months to years after continuous exposure to specific pharmacological agents, resolving upon prompt drug discontinuation.

High-risk causative drugs with definite evidence include procainamide (up to 20% incidence, highest risk) and hydralazine (5% to 8% incidence); moderate-risk drugs include minocycline, diltiazem, quinidine, and penicillamine.

Hepatic N-acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2) slow acetylator phenotype confers marked genetic susceptibility to procainamide- and hydralazine-induced lupus due to delayed drug clearance and prolonged accumulation of reactive toxic hydroxylamine metabolites.

Anti-histone antibodies are positive in >95% to 100% of classic systemic drug-induced lupus (specifically targeting the H2A-H2B histone dimer in procainamide/hydralazine DILE); however, anti-histone antibodies are non-specific and occur in 50% of idiopathic SLE.

Antibodies highly specific for idiopathic SLE (anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm) and severe hypocomplementemia are characteristically absent in classic drug-induced lupus, with the notable exception of anti-TNF inhibitor-induced lupus.

Clinical hallmarks of systemic DILE feature constitutional symptoms (fever, fatigue, weight loss), symmetrical polyarthralgias/polyarthritis, and serositis (pleurisy, pericarditis); severe renal and central nervous system disease are characteristically rare.
