Drug-induced subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (DI-SCLE) manifests as widespread annular or papulosquamous sun-exposed lesions with positive anti-Ro/SSA antibodies, classically triggered by terbinafine, thiazide diuretics, calcium channel blockers, proton pump inhibitors, and checkpoint inhibitors.

Definitive management requires immediate, permanent cessation of the offending drug; symptoms typically resolve over several weeks to months, with temporary low-dose oral glucocorticoids used for active serositis or arthritis while awaiting clearance.

topics.title: Antiphospholipid syndrome
mustKnow: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is an autoimmune thrombophilia characterized by vascular thrombosis (arterial, venous, or microvascular) and/or pregnancy morbidity, occurring as primary APS or secondary to another autoimmune disease (predominantly systemic lupus erythematosus).

The 2023 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for APS employ an entry criterion requiring at least one positive antiphospholipid antibody test within 3 years of an APS-associated clinical event, evaluated across weighted clinical domains (venous thromboembolism, arterial thrombosis, microvascular domains, obstetric domains) and laboratory domains, requiring >=3 points in both clinical and laboratory domains.

The classical laboratory criteria antibodies are lupus anticoagulant (LA), anticardiolipin (aCL) IgG/IgM, and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I (anti-beta2GPI) IgG/IgM; a positive test must be confirmed on two or more occasions at least 12 weeks apart to exclude transient post-infectious antibodies.

The 'triple-positive' antiphospholipid profile denotes simultaneous presence of lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin IgG, and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I IgG; it represents the highest risk phenotype for recurrent arterial and venous thrombosis, pregnancy loss, and progression to catastrophic APS.

Lupus anticoagulant testing follows a mandatory multi-step algorithm: initial screening prolongation of a phospholipid-dependent clotting assay (e.g., dilute Russell viper venom time [dRVVT] or sensitive aPTT), failure to correct prolongation upon 1:1 mixing with normal platelet-poor plasma, and definitive correction upon addition of excess confirmatory phospholipids.

First-line secondary antithrombotic prophylaxis for definitive venous thromboembolism in APS is therapeutic anticoagulation with vitamin K antagonists (warfarin) titrated to a target INR of 2.0 to 3.0; randomized controlled trials (TRAPS and ASTRO-APS) demonstrated that direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs, e.g., rivaroxaban) are inferior and confer excess arterial thrombotic risk in triple-positive APS.

Obstetric APS clinical criteria include >=3 unexplained consecutive spontaneous abortions before the 10th week of gestation, >=1 unexplained fetal death of a morphologically normal fetus at or beyond the 10th week, or >=1 premature birth of a normal neonate before the 34th week due to severe preeclampsia, eclampsia, or placental insufficiency.

Standard management of confirmed obstetric APS during pregnancy is combined prophylaxis with low-dose aspirin (75 to 100 mg daily) starting preconception and prophylactic-dose low molecular weight heparin (LMWH, e.g., enoxaparin 40 mg daily) initiated as soon as intrauterine pregnancy is confirmed, continued throughout gestation and for 6 weeks postpartum.

topics.title: Sjogren disease
mustKnow: Sjogren disease is a chronic systemic autoimmune exocrinopathy characterized by lymphocytic infiltration of salivary and lacrimal glands, resulting in xerostomia (dry mouth) and keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes), occurring primarily in perimenopausal women.

The 2016 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for primary Sjogren syndrome apply to patients with ocular or oral dryness or suspicion of systemic disease; a score >=4 points confirms classification based on weighted criteria: focal lymphocytic sialadenitis on minor salivary gland biopsy (focus score >=1 per 4 mm2, 3 points), positive anti-SSA/Ro (3 points), ocular staining score >=5 or van Bijsterveld score >=4 (1 point), Schirmer test <=5 mm/5 min (1 point), and unstimulated whole saliva flow <=0.1 mL/min (1 point).

Minor salivary gland labial lip biopsy requires histopathologic demonstration of focal lymphocytic sialadenitis, defined by a focus score of 1 or more (a focus is an aggregate of 50 or more mononuclear inflammatory cells, predominantly CD4+ T cells, adjacent to normal-appearing acinar units) in a 4 square millimeter tissue area.

Anti-Ro/SSA antibodies are positive in 60% to 70% of primary Sjogren patients, whereas anti-La/SSB antibodies (found in 30% to 40%) are almost never present without anti-Ro; isolated anti-La is non-specific and excluded from the 2016 classification criteria.

Systemic extraglandular manifestations occur in over 30% of Sjogren patients: cutaneous purpura, non-erosive polyarthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, interstitial lung disease (LIP and NSIP), interstitial nephritis, distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis, and small-fiber sensory ganglionopathy.

Patients with primary Sjogren disease face a 15- to 30-fold increased lifetime relative risk of developing non-Hodgkin lymphoma, most commonly mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) marginal zone B-cell lymphoma of the salivary glands; major clinical predictors include persistent parotid enlargement, cutaneous purpura, cryoglobulinemia, hypocomplementemia (low C4), and monoclonal gammopathy.

Symptomatic treatment of glandular dryness includes preservative-free artificial tears and ocular lubricants, oral muscarinic acetylcholine receptor agonists (pilocarpine 5 mg three to four times daily, or cevimeline 30 mg three times daily) which stimulate remaining functional acinar secretions, alongside meticulous dental hygiene.

Systemic immunomodulatory therapy is guided by the EULAR Sjogren's Syndrome Disease Activity Index (ESSDAI); hydroxychloroquine is effective for arthralgias and fatigue, whereas severe extraglandular organ involvement (vasculitis, glomerulonephritis, severe neuropathy) mandates systemic glucocorticoids combined with rituximab, cyclophosphamide, or mycophenolate mofetil.

topics.title: Systemic sclerosis classification and skin disease
mustKnow: Systemic sclerosis is classified into limited cutaneous SSc (lcSSc, skin thickening distal to elbows and knees, and face) and diffuse cutaneous SSc (dcSSc, skin thickening extending proximal to elbows and knees, involving chest, abdomen, or upper arms) by LeRoy criteria.

The 2013 ACR/EULAR classification criteria classify patients with a cumulative score >=9 points; skin thickening of the fingers extending proximal to the metacarpophalangeal joints is a sufficient standalone criterion (scoring 9 points).

Skin involvement progresses through three stages: an early edematous ('puffy fingers') phase, an indurative phase with dermal thickening, and a late atrophic phase; tracked objectively by the modified Rodnan skin score (mRSS, 0 to 51 points).

Diffuse cutaneous SSc is strongly linked to anti-topoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) and anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies, featuring rapid skin progression, early internal organ involvement (ILD, renal crisis), and higher mortality.

Limited cutaneous SSc encompasses the CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia), associates with anti-centromere antibodies (ACA), and carries a late risk of isolated pulmonary arterial hypertension.

Anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies identify diffuse SSc with rapid skin thickening, tendon friction rubs, heightened risk of acute scleroderma renal crisis (in up to 25%), and a striking close temporal association with synchronous malignancy.

Nailfold capillaroscopy demonstrates the diagnostic scleroderma pattern: early giant capillary loops (>50 micrometers), active microhemorrhages, capillary dropout with avascular areas, and late neoangiogenic ramified arborization.

Systemic sclerosis sine scleroderma is a recognized clinical subset occurring in <5% of patients, characterized by characteristic internal organ disease (esophageal dysmotility, ILD, PAH, renal crisis) and positive SSc autoantibodies in the complete absence of cutaneous skin thickening.

topics.title: Organ complications of systemic sclerosis
mustKnow: Interstitial lung disease (SSc-ILD) affects >80% of diffuse SSc and 30% of limited SSc; HRCT chest shows non-specific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) with basilar ground-glass opacities and traction bronchiectasis, managed with mycophenolate mofetil or nintedanib.

Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH, Group 1 PH) affects 10% to 15% of systemic sclerosis patients, diagnosed by right heart catheterization (mPAP >20 mmHg, PCWP <=15 mmHg, PVR >2 Wood units), treated with endothelin receptor antagonists and PDE-5 inhibitors.

Scleroderma renal crisis (SRC) is an acute hypertensive emergency in 5% to 10% of diffuse SSc patients, triggered by glucocorticoids (prednisone >=15 mg/day) and anti-RNA polymerase III, requiring emergency treatment with oral captopril.

Gastrointestinal involvement affects >90% of SSc patients: lower esophageal sphincter incompetence leads to severe gastroesophageal reflux and Barrett esophagus, while gastric antral vascular ectasia ('watermelon stomach') causes chronic iron deficiency anemia.

Small intestinal dysmotility causes pseudo-obstruction and small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO), presenting with chronic watery diarrhea, bloating, and malabsorption, diagnosed by hydrogen breath testing and treated with rotating courses of rifaximin.

Myocardial fibrosis in diffuse SSc causes patchy contraction band necrosis, diastolic dysfunction, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), and ventricular arrhythmias, identified by late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac MRI.

Calcinosis cutis represents dystrophic subcutaneous and periarticular calcium hydroxyapatite deposition, complicated by chronic painful ulcerations and secondary infections, managed with surgical debridement, diltiazem, or sodium thiosulfate.

Autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (AHSCT) preceded by immunoablative conditioning improves skin scores, pulmonary function, and long-term event-free survival in rapidly progressive, poor-prognosis diffuse SSc failing conventional DMARDs.

topics.title: Raynaud phenomenon
mustKnow: Raynaud phenomenon is an episodic, reversible digital vasospasm provoked by cold temperatures or emotional stress, presenting with classical triphasic color changes: pallor (white, ischemic arteriolar vasospasm), cyanosis (blue, tissue deoxygenation), and rubor (red, reactive hyperemic reperfusion).

Primary Raynaud phenomenon (Raynaud disease) is idiopathic, occurring in young women (15 to 30 years), characterized by symmetric episodic attacks, normal physical examination, absence of digital tissue necrosis or ulceration, normal nailfold capillaroscopy, and negative ANA.

Secondary Raynaud phenomenon is caused by an underlying systemic disease (most commonly systemic sclerosis, SLE, MCTD); clinical clues include onset after age 30, painful asymmetric attacks, digital pitting scars, tissue necrosis or gangrene, abnormal nailfold capillaroscopy, and positive ANA.

Nailfold capillaroscopy at 200x magnification distinguishes primary from secondary Raynaud: the presence of enlarged or giant capillary loops (>50 micrometers) and avascular areas has >90% predictive value for the evolution of systemic sclerosis or scleroderma spectrum disorders.

Lifestyle and non-pharmacological measures are the essential first-line foundation: total-body cold avoidance, layered warm clothing, thermal mittens, chemical hand warmers, avoidance of emotional stress, and strict cessation of tobacco and sympathomimetic drugs.

Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (oral nifedipine 30 to 60 mg daily or amlodipine) are the first-line pharmacological treatment of choice, significantly reducing the frequency and severity of vasospastic attacks.

Phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5) inhibitors (sildenafil 20 mg three times daily or tadalafil) are effective add-on or alternative therapy for severe Raynaud phenomenon refractory to calcium channel blockers, significantly improving digital microvascular blood flow.

For severe digital ischemia, critical digital ulcers, or impending gangrene, intravenous prostacyclin analogs (iloprost infusions) are the most effective therapy, accelerating ulcer healing; oral bosentan (endothelin receptor antagonist) is approved to prevent the recurrence of new digital ulcers.

topics.title: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies
mustKnow: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies are characterized by immune-mediated striated muscle inflammation causing symmetrical, predominantly proximal muscle weakness, elevated serum muscle enzymes (creatine kinase, aldolase, transaminases), and electromyographic irritability.

Dermatomyositis displays pathognomonic cutaneous findings: Gottron papules (violaceous papules over MCP and PIP joints), Gottron sign, heliotrope rash (violaceous periorbital erythema and edema), shawl sign, and V-neck sign, with muscle biopsy showing perifascicular myofiber atrophy.

Polymyositis lacks cutaneous signs, characteristically presenting in adults with subacute proximal limb-girdle weakness, with biopsy demonstrating endomysial infiltration of non-necrotic myofibers by clonally expanded CD8+ cytotoxic T cells expressing perforin.

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) features severe acute or subacute proximal weakness with massive CK elevations (>10,000 to 20,000 U/L), pauci-immune myofiber necrosis on biopsy, and high-affinity autoantibodies against SRP or HMG-CoA reductase (anti-HMGCR, associated with statins).

Inclusion body myositis (IBM) affects men older than 50 years, causing asymmetric weakness of deep finger flexors (forearm) and quadriceps; muscle biopsy reveals basophilic rimmed vacuoles, amyloid deposits, and TDP-43 inclusions, running an indolent course refractory to immunosuppression.

Antisynthetase syndrome encompasses myositis, interstitial lung disease, Raynaud phenomenon, non-erosive polyarthritis, and mechanic's hands in the presence of anti-aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase autoantibodies (anti-Jo-1, anti-PL-7, anti-PL-12).

Adult dermatomyositis carries a 3- to 6-fold increased risk of underlying internal malignancy; anti-TIF1-gamma and anti-NXP2 autoantibodies identify cancer-associated myositis in up to 50% of adult patients, mandating extensive age-appropriate cancer screening.

First-line induction therapy combines high-dose systemic glucocorticoids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day or IV pulse methylprednisolone) with steroid-sparing immunosuppressants (methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil), adding IVIG (2 g/kg monthly) for refractory disease or IMNM.

topics.title: Mixed connective tissue disease and overlap syndromes
mustKnow: Mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD, Sharp syndrome) is an overlap autoimmune disorder characterized by overlapping clinical features of systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis, occurring in the presence of extremely high titers of autoantibodies against U1-small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (U1-snRNP).

High-titer anti-U1-RNP antibodies (specifically recognizing the 68-kDa, A, and C proteins of the spliceosome) are mandatory for diagnosis in all validated classification criteria (Alarcon-Segovia, Kasukawa, Sharp); the virtual absence of antibodies specific for other diseases (anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, anti-Scl-70) is essential to maintain the distinct diagnosis of MCTD.

The cardinal clinical presentation of MCTD includes almost universal Raynaud phenomenon (>95%), diffuse puffy swelling of the hands ('sausage fingers'), non-erosive inflammatory polyarthritis, esophageal hypomotility, and mild inflammatory myopathy with elevated muscle enzymes.

Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is the most frequent disease-related cause of mortality in MCTD, developing in up to 15% to 25% of patients, often with an insidious onset and in the absence of severe interstitial lung disease, mandating annual non-invasive echocardiographic screening.

Severe progressive renal disease is characteristically uncommon in pure MCTD compared to SLE; when renal disease occurs, it most commonly manifests as membranous nephropathy or mild mesangial glomerulonephritis, whereas diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis is rare and suggests transition to definitive SLE.

Over decades of longitudinal follow-up, up to 30% to 50% of patients initially classified as MCTD evolve or differentiate into another single, well-defined systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease, most commonly systemic sclerosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, or Sjogren disease.

Scleromyositis represents a classic overlap syndrome displaying combined clinical and histopathologic features of systemic sclerosis and inflammatory myositis; it is strongly identified by autoantibodies against PM-Scl (PM-Scl-75 and PM-Scl-100) or anti-Ku, presenting with proximal muscle weakness, mechanic's hands, sclerodactyly, and severe ILD.

Pharmacological therapy for MCTD is directed at the dominant organ manifestation: mild arthritis, serositis, and puffy hands respond well to hydroxychloroquine and low-to-moderate dose glucocorticoids, whereas severe myositis, rapidly progressive ILD, or severe organ disease require aggressive immunosuppressants (mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide).

topics.title: IgG4-related disease
mustKnow: IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD) is a fibroinflammatory condition characterized by mass-forming tumefactive lesions, tissue-infiltrating IgG4-positive plasma cells, and progressive storiform fibrosis, capable of involving nearly every organ system.

The 2019 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for IgG4-RD establish a three-step validation process: mandatory entry criteria (typical clinical/radiologic organ involvement), exclusion criteria, and a weighted scoring system requiring >=20 points.

The definitive histopathologic triad of IgG4-RD consists of: (1) dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate rich in IgG4+ plasma cells; (2) storiform fibrosis (cartwheel-like whorled collagen pattern); and (3) obliterative phlebitis (venous lumen obliteration by inflammatory cells).

Immunohistochemical criteria require an absolute count of IgG4-positive plasma cells exceeding organ-specific cutoffs (typically >10 to 50 per HPF) AND a ratio of IgG4-positive to total IgG-positive plasma cells exceeding 40%.

Serum IgG4 concentrations are elevated (>135 mg/dL) in up to 60% to 70% of active cases; however, elevated serum IgG4 is neither sensitive nor specific, and normal serum IgG4 does not exclude the diagnosis.

Classic organ manifestations of IgG4-RD include Type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis (painless jaundice, sausage-shaped pancreas with hypoattenuating rim), Mikulicz disease (lacrimal and salivary gland enlargement), and Riedel thyroiditis.

Retroperitoneal fibrosis in IgG4-RD manifests as a fibroinflammatory soft tissue mantle encasing the infrarenal abdominal aorta and iliac vessels, characteristically producing medial ureteral deviation, hydronephrosis, and post-renal azotemia.

Systemic glucocorticoids (oral prednisone 0.6 to 0.8 mg/kg/day) are the standard first-line remission induction therapy, producing rapid tumefactive regression; for refractory disease or maintenance, B-cell depletion with rituximab is the targeted biologic of choice.

topics.title: Connective tissue disease associated ILD
mustKnow: Connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease (CTD-ILD) is a major contributor to morbidity and mortality, occurring most frequently in systemic sclerosis (SSc, up to 80%), rheumatoid arthritis (RA, 10% to 30%), and inflammatory myopathies/antisynthetase syndrome (up to 70%).

High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest is the gold standard diagnostic modality: non-specific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP, basilar ground-glass opacities, reticulation, traction bronchiectasis) is the predominant pattern in SSc, myositis, and SLE, whereas usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP, subpleural honeycombing) predominates in RA.

Pulmonary function testing (PFT) classically reveals a restrictive ventilatory defect with reduced forced vital capacity (FVC) and impaired gas transfer manifested by decreased diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO).

The Scleroderma Lung Study II (SLS II) established that oral mycophenolate mofetil (MMF, target dose 3 g daily for 2 years) is equivalent in preserving FVC to 1 year of oral cyclophosphamide, with substantially superior safety, positioning MMF as first-line immunosuppressive therapy for CTD-ILD.

The SENSCIS trial in SSc-ILD and the INBUILD trial across progressive fibrosing CTD-ILDs proved that nintedanib (an oral tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting PDGF, FGF, and VEGF receptors, 150 mg twice daily) significantly reduced the annual rate of FVC decline by 44% to 57%.

The focuSSced trial and phase 3 data demonstrated that tocilizumab (monoclonal anti-IL-6 receptor antibody) significantly stabilized forced vital capacity in early active diffuse SSc with elevated acute-phase reactants, gaining regulatory approval for SSc-ILD.

Antisynthetase syndrome ILD is characterized by rapid pulmonary progression with anti-tRNA synthetase antibodies (anti-Jo-1, anti-PL-7, anti-PL-12); treatment combines high-dose systemic glucocorticoids with mycophenolate, tacrolimus, or rituximab.

Progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF) is defined by meeting at least 2 of 3 criteria (worsening respiratory symptoms, physiological decline in FVC >=5% or DLCO >=10%, and radiological progression on HRCT) within the past year, qualifying patients for add-on antifibrotic therapy.

topics.title: Pulmonary arterial hypertension in connective tissue disease
mustKnow: Pulmonary hypertension complicating connective tissue diseases (CTD-PH) represents a devastating vascular complication; Group 1 pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) occurs predominantly in systemic sclerosis, mixed connective tissue disease, and SLE, carrying higher mortality than idiopathic PAH.

Definitive diagnosis requires right heart catheterization (RHC): hemodynamic criteria per 2022 ESC/ERS guidelines define pre-capillary pulmonary arterial hypertension as mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) >20 mmHg, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) <=15 mmHg, and pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) >2 Wood units.

Screening for PAH is recommended annually in all patients with systemic sclerosis using the two-step DETECT algorithm (incorporating clinical variables, PFT, serum NT-proBNP, and ECG) or resting transthoracic echocardiography (tricuspid regurgitant jet velocity >2.8 m/s).

Pulmonary function testing showing an isolated disproportionate reduction in diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO <60% predicted) with preserved forced vital capacity (FVC/DLCO ratio >1.6 to 1.8) is a strong clinical clue for underlying pulmonary vascular disease.

Initial therapy for low-to-intermediate risk CTD-PAH relies on upfront oral combination therapy pairing an endothelin receptor antagonist (ERA: ambrisentan, macitentan, or bosentan) with a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor (PDE-5i: tadalafil or sildenafil).

For high-risk CTD-PAH patients (WHO functional class IV, cardiac index <2.0 L/min/m2, right ventricular failure), upfront combination therapy including continuous intravenous prostacyclin analogs (epoprostenol or subcutaneous treprostinil) is mandatory to prevent cardiovascular collapse.

Group 3 pulmonary hypertension (PH due to lung disease and hypoxia) frequently coexists in CTD patients with underlying fibrosing interstitial lung disease; treatment requires optimizing underlying CTD-ILD and supplemental oxygen, as pulmonary vasodilators carry the risk of worsening ventilation-perfusion mismatch and hypoxemia.

Inhaled treprostinil is FDA-approved for pulmonary hypertension associated with interstitial lung disease (PH-ILD) based on the INCREASE trial, which demonstrated significant improvements in 6-minute walk distance and reduction in NT-proBNP without worsening ventilation-perfusion mismatch.

topics.title: Classification and assessment of vasculitis
mustKnow: The 2012 Revised Chapel Hill Consensus Conference (CHCC) establishes nomenclature for systemic vasculitides based on predominant vessel caliber: large vessel (Takayasu, GCA), medium vessel (PAN, Kawasaki), and small vessel (ANCA-associated and immune complex).

Small-vessel vasculitis is divided into ANCA-associated vasculitides (pauci-immune: microscopic polyangiitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, eosinophilic GPA) and immune complex vasculitides (anti-GBM disease, cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, IgA vasculitis, hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis).
Variable-vessel vasculitis is defined as systemic vasculitis capable of affecting vessels of any size (arteries, veins, and capillaries), classic examples being Behcet disease and Cogan syndrome.

Single-organ vasculitis (SOV) affects arteries or veins in a single organ without systemic involvement, including primary angiitis of the CNS, cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis, and isolated testicular vasculitis.

Vasculitis associated with systemic disease includes lupus vasculitis, rheumatoid vasculitis, and sarcoid vasculitis; secondary vasculitis associated with probable etiology includes hepatitis B virus-associated PAN and hepatitis C virus-associated cryoglobulinemia.

The 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria provide separate, validated, scoring-based criteria sets for GPA, MPA, EGPA, Takayasu arteritis, and GCA, reflecting modern imaging, ANCA serology, and clinical features.

The Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score (BVAS v3) evaluates 64 items across nine organ systems to distinguish active ongoing vasculitis from permanent chronic irreversible damage captured by the Vasculitis Damage Index (VDI).

The Five-Factor Score (FFS, revised 2009) predicts 5-year mortality in necrotizing vasculitides based on age >65, cardiac involvement, gastrointestinal involvement, renal insufficiency (creatinine >=150 micromol/L), and absence of ENT signs.

topics.title: Giant cell arteritis and polymyalgia rheumatica
mustKnow: Giant cell arteritis (GCA, temporal arteritis) is a chronic granulomatous panarteritis of medium- and large-sized arteries that occurs exclusively in individuals aged 50 years or older (incidence peaking between 70 and 80 years), with a strong female predilection (3:1).

The 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for giant cell arteritis establish age >=50 years as an absolute entry criterion; a cumulative score >=6 points confirms classification based on weighted clinical domains (morning stiffness, jaw claudication, vision loss, scalp tenderness, abnormal temporal artery exam), laboratory domains (ESR >=50 mm/h or CRP >=10 mg/L), and imaging/biopsy domains.

Jaw claudication (fatigue and cramping pain in masseter and temporalis muscles when chewing, caused by maxillary artery branch ischemia) is the most specific clinical symptom of cranial GCA, conferring a likelihood ratio >4.0 for positive temporal artery biopsy.

Permanent visual loss is the most feared catastrophic complication of GCA, occurring in 15% to 20% of untreated patients, most commonly due to anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (AION) caused by occlusion of the short posterior ciliary arteries, presenting with sudden, painless, irreversible altitudinal visual field deficit and pale swollen optic disc.

Temporal artery biopsy remains the histopathologic reference standard, demonstrating transmural granulomatous inflammation, mononuclear cell infiltration, disruption and fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina, multinucleated giant cells, and intimal hyperplasia; due to 'skip lesions', a surgical specimen length of at least 1 to 2 cm should be excised.

Color Doppler ultrasound of temporal and axillary arteries is the preferred first-line imaging modality; the 'halo sign' (a non-compressible, homogeneous hypoechoic wall thickening surrounding the perfused lumen) has a pooled sensitivity of 75% and specificity exceeding 95% in experienced centers.

Emergency therapy with high-dose systemic glucocorticoids (oral prednisone 40 to 60 mg/day; or intravenous pulse methylprednisolone 500 to 1,000 mg daily for 3 days if visual symptoms or amaurosis fugax are present) must be initiated immediately upon clinical suspicion, without waiting for temporal artery biopsy.

The GiACTA trial proved that the IL-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab (162 mg subcutaneously weekly or every 2 weeks) combined with a standardized 26-week prednisone taper produced significantly higher sustained glucocorticoid-free remission (56% vs 14% at 52 weeks) and markedly reduced cumulative glucocorticoid exposure, gaining FDA/EMA approval for GCA.

topics.title: Takayasu arteritis
mustKnow: Takayasu arteritis (pulseless disease) is a chronic granulomatous panarteritis predominantly affecting the aorta, its primary branches (subclavian, carotid, renal), and the pulmonary arteries, occurring characteristically in young females under 40 years of age.

The 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for Takayasu arteritis require age at onset <=60 years and imaging evidence of large vessel vasculitis as mandatory entry criteria, confirmed by accumulating >=5 points across clinical domains (pulse deficit, claudication, arterial bruits, blood pressure asymmetry >20 mmHg) and imaging domains (luminal narrowing, occlusion, wall thickening).

The Hata angiographic classification categorizes Takayasu arteritis into six anatomical types based on vascular involvement: Type I (branches of the aortic arch only), Type IIa (ascending aorta, aortic arch, and branches), Type IIb (Type IIa plus thoracic descending aorta), Type III (thoracic descending aorta, abdominal aorta, and/or renal arteries), Type IV (abdominal aorta and/or renal arteries), and Type V (combined features of Type IIb and IV, the most common type).

Renal artery stenosis occurs in 30% to 50% of Takayasu patients, typically ostial or proximal, activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system to produce severe renovascular hypertension, which may be masked if blood pressure is measured in claudicating, pulseless upper extremities.

Cardiovascular complications represent the principal determinants of mortality: severe aortic regurgitation from inflammatory aortic root and valve ring dilatation (in up to 25%), coronary ostial stenosis from ascending aortitis, congestive heart failure, and pulmonary arterial hypertension from pulmonary branch vasculitis.

Non-invasive vascular imaging by magnetic resonance angiography (MRA), CT angiography (CTA), or 18F-FDG PET-CT has replaced conventional catheter digital subtraction angiography; MRA detects early mural edema (concentric vessel wall thickening and delayed mural enhancement) prior to fixed luminal stenosis.

First-line medical induction therapy requires high-dose systemic glucocorticoids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day); however, because relapses occur in over 50% to 70% during steroid tapering, early initiation of steroid-sparing immunosuppressants (methotrexate, azathioprine, leflunomide, or mycophenolate mofetil) is recommended.

For relapsing or refractory Takayasu arteritis, biological therapy with monoclonal anti-TNF agents (infliximab, adalimumab) or the IL-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab demonstrates substantial steroid-sparing efficacy and arrests vascular lesion progression; surgical or endovascular revascularization must strictly be delayed until systemic inflammatory activity is quiescent.

topics.title: Polyarteritis nodosa
mustKnow: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is a systemic necrotizing arteritis predominantly affecting medium- and small-sized muscular arteries, characteristically sparing the pulmonary arterial circulation and the microvasculature (arterioles, capillaries, venules), with no association with ANCA.

The 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for polyarteritis nodosa require biopsy confirmation of necrotizing arteritis or angiographic aneurysms/occlusions with accumulated score >=5 points across weighted domains including mononeuritis multiplex, motor neuropathy, testicular pain, livedo reticularis, renal insufficiency, and abdominal symptoms.

Secondary polyarteritis nodosa is historically linked to active Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in up to 30% of global cases, where circulating HBsAg-anti-HBs immune complexes deposit in arterial walls within the first 6 months of acute HBV infection.

Renal involvement in PAN is driven by renal artery vasculitis and ischemia causing severe renin-mediated renovascular hypertension and renal infarcts; true glomerulonephritis is absent because glomerular capillaries are small vessels spared by PAN.

Visceral catheter angiography or CT angiography demonstrates microaneurysms (typically 1 to 5 mm in diameter) and stenoses affecting branching points of the renal, mesenteric, and hepatic medium-sized arteries, creating the classic 'beads-on-a-string' appearance.

Gastrointestinal involvement presents with postprandial abdominal angina, bowel ischemia, transmural infarction, and spontaneous visceral perforation, representing a major contributor to vasculitis-associated mortality and scoring on the Five-Factor Score.

First-line induction therapy for severe idiopathic PAN (FFS >=1) combines high-dose systemic glucocorticoids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day or IV pulse methylprednisolone) with intravenous cyclophosphamide; mild non-organ-threatening disease (FFS = 0) can be initiated on glucocorticoid monotherapy.

Management of HBV-associated PAN fundamentally differs from idiopathic PAN: a short, time-limited course of glucocorticoids and plasma exchange is combined with immediate potent antiviral therapy (entecavir or tenofovir), avoiding long-term cytotoxic immunosuppression which promotes viral replication and hepatic failure.

topics.title: Kawasaki disease
mustKnow: Kawasaki disease is an acute, self-limited febrile systemic medium-vessel necrotizing vasculitis of unknown etiology predominantly affecting infants and young children (<5 years of age in >85%), representing the leading cause of acquired pediatric heart disease in developed countries.

Classical diagnostic criteria require persistent high fever lasting >=5 days plus at least 4 of 5 principal clinical features: bilateral non-exudative bulbar conjunctival injection, oral mucosal changes (strawberry tongue, erythema, fissured lips), polymorphous non-vesicular rash, peripheral extremity changes (erythema, indurative edema, periungual desquamation), and cervical lymphadenopathy (>=1.5 cm, usually unilateral).

Coronary artery aneurysms (CAA) develop in up to 25% of untreated children, carrying risks of myocardial infarction, ischemic heart disease, and sudden cardiac death; coronary dimensions must be normalized to body surface area and expressed as echocardiographic Z-scores.

Coronary aneurysm severity is stratified by luminal dimensions and Z-scores: dilation only (Z-score 2 to <2.5), small aneurysm (Z-score 2.5 to <5), medium aneurysm (Z-score 5 to <10 and absolute dimension <8 mm), and giant aneurysm (Z-score >=10 or absolute internal diameter >=8 mm).

Standard primary therapy is a single high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) infusion at 2 g/kg administered over 10 to 12 hours, initiated within the first 10 days of fever onset, which dramatically reduces the incidence of coronary artery aneurysms from 25% to <4% to 5%.

Aspirin is co-administered initially at moderate-to-high anti-inflammatory doses (30 to 50 mg/kg/day or 80 to 100 mg/kg/day) until the child has been afebrile for 48 to 72 hours, then transitioned to low-dose antiplatelet maintenance (3 to 5 mg/kg/day) for 6 to 8 weeks if coronaries are normal.

IVIG resistance (defined as persistent or recrudescent fever >=36 hours after completion of the initial IVIG infusion) occurs in 10% to 20% of patients; risk scores (Kobayashi, Egami) identify high-risk patients who benefit from upfront primary adjuvant systemic glucocorticoids.

For refractory IVIG-resistant Kawasaki disease, recommended secondary therapeutic options include a second dose of IVIG (2 g/kg), high-dose intravenous pulse methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg for 3 days), or infliximab (monoclonal anti-TNF antibody, 5 mg/kg), which rapidly quenches persistent systemic vascular inflammation.

topics.title: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
mustKnow: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA, formerly Wegener granulomatosis) is a systemic necrotizing granulomatous small- and medium-vessel vasculitis characterized by the classical clinical triad of upper respiratory tract, lower respiratory tract, and renal involvement.

Over 85% to 90% of patients with generalized active GPA possess cytoplasmic ANCA (c-ANCA) directed against proteinase 3 (PR3-ANCA); PR3-ANCA binds cell-surface PR3 on primed neutrophils, triggering inappropriate degranulation, respiratory burst, and endothelial necrosis.

Upper airway manifestations occur in >90% of GPA patients, including chronic refractory rhinosinusitis, epistaxis, nasal mucosal crusting, destructive nasal septal perforation resulting in 'saddle-nose' deformity, conductive/sensorineural hearing loss, and dangerous subglottic stenosis.

Pulmonary involvement features multiple bilateral nodular lung lesions (which cavitate with thick, irregular walls in up to 50% on CT), alveolar consolidations, and life-threatening diffuse alveolar hemorrhage due to necrotizing pulmonary capillaritis.

Renal disease is characterized by pauci-immune necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis; light microscopy shows cellular crescents, fibrinoid necrosis, and absence of significant immune complex deposition on immunofluorescence.

The landmark RAVE trial established that rituximab (375 mg/m2 weekly for 4 doses) is non-inferior to daily oral cyclophosphamide for induction of remission in severe ANCA-associated vasculitis, and significantly superior in patients presenting with relapsing disease.

The ADVOCATE trial demonstrated that avacopan, an oral selective complement C5a receptor (C5aR1) antagonist (30 mg twice daily), was superior to a standard tapering prednisone regimen in sustained remission at week 52 while eliminating glucocorticoid-associated toxicities.

Maintenance therapy with rituximab (500 mg every 6 months for at least 18 to 24 months, proven superior to azathioprine in the MAINRITSAN trial) is standard of care; all patients receiving rituximab or cyclophosphamide mandate Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

topics.title: Microscopic polyangiitis and AAV management
mustKnow: Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) is a systemic necrotizing small-vessel vasculitis without granulomatous inflammation, characteristically presenting with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary capillaritis causing diffuse alveolar hemorrhage.

Approximately 70% to 85% of MPA patients have circulating perinuclear ANCA (p-ANCA) targeting myeloperoxidase (MPO-ANCA); anti-MPO antibodies stimulate neutrophil oxidative burst, degranulation, and endothelial cell lysis.

Renal involvement occurs in >90% of MPA patients, manifesting as pauci-immune necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis; light microscopy shows segmental fibrinoid necrosis and crescents with absent immune complexes on immunofluorescence.

Unlike granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), microscopic polyangiitis is clinically distinguished by the complete absence of destructive upper respiratory granulomatous inflammation (no saddle-nose deformity, no cavitary lung nodules, and no subglottic stenosis).

Fibrosing interstitial lung disease (ILD) with a usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) or NSIP pattern occurs in up to 15% to 30% of MPO-ANCA positive MPA patients, often preceding vasculitic manifestations and carrying a high mortality.

First-line induction therapy for organ- or life-threatening MPA combines high-dose systemic glucocorticoids with either rituximab (375 mg/m2 weekly for 4 doses) or intravenous cyclophosphamide, both demonstrating equivalent remission induction.

The PEXIVAS randomized trial demonstrated that routine therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) did not reduce death or end-stage renal disease in severe AAV with renal failure (serum creatinine >=5.7 mg/dL) or alveolar hemorrhage, leading guidelines to restrict plasma exchange to concurrent anti-GBM disease or refractory DAH.

Remission maintenance relies on low-dose rituximab (500 mg every 6 months) or oral azathioprine (2 mg/kg/day) continued for at least 24 months, alongside mandatory trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis.

topics.title: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
mustKnow: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA, Churg-Strauss syndrome) is a necrotizing systemic vasculitis characterized by severe adult-onset asthma, blood and tissue eosinophilia, and necrotizing granulomatous inflammation affecting small-to-medium vessels.

EGPA classically progresses through three clinical phases: an allergic/prodromal phase (adult-onset asthma, allergic rhinitis, nasal polyposis), an eosinophilic phase (peripheral blood eosinophilia >1,500/microL or >10%, eosinophilic pneumonia, gastroenteritis), and a systemic vasculitic phase (mononeuritis multiplex, purpura, glomerulonephritis).

ANCA positivity occurs in 30% to 50% of EGPA patients, almost exclusively p-ANCA targeting myeloperoxidase (MPO-ANCA); ANCA-positive disease features prominent vasculitic manifestations (glomerulonephritis, mononeuritis multiplex, purpura), whereas ANCA-negative disease exhibits marked eosinophilic tissue infiltration with severe cardiac involvement.

Cardiac involvement is the leading cause of mortality in EGPA, manifesting as eosinophilic endomyocarditis, myocardial fibrosis, restrictive cardiomyopathy, intracardiac thrombi, and congestive heart failure, visible on cardiac MRI as late gadolinium enhancement.

Peripheral neuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex or asymmetric polyneuropathy) is the most frequent vasculitic manifestation of EGPA, occurring in up to 70% to 80% of patients due to ischemic epineurial arteritis.

Risk stratification by the Five-Factor Score (FFS) guides therapy: patients with severe organ- or life-threatening disease (FFS >=1, e.g., cardiomyopathy, GI involvement, renal insufficiency) require combined induction with systemic glucocorticoids and intravenous cyclophosphamide.

Mepolizumab, a fully humanized monoclonal antibody targeting IL-5 (300 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks), was shown in the MIRRA trial to significantly increase weeks in remission and enable dramatic glucocorticoid tapering in relapsing or refractory non-organ-threatening EGPA.

Benralizumab, an anti-IL-5 receptor alpha monoclonal antibody that induces direct antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity of eosinophils, proved non-inferior to mepolizumab in the MANDARA trial for achieving sustained remission in EGPA.

topics.title: IgA vasculitis and urticarial vasculitis
mustKnow: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura) is an immune complex small-vessel vasculitis characterized by galactose-deficient IgA1 (Gd-IgA1) deposition in skin, joints, intestines, and glomeruli, predominantly affecting children aged 3 to 10 years.

The clinical tetrad of IgA vasculitis comprises non-thrombocytopenic palpable purpura (with lower extremity/buttock predilection), colicky abdominal pain (with risk of ileo-ileal intussusception), arthralgias/arthritis, and glomerulonephritis.

Renal biopsy in IgA vasculitis displays mesangial proliferation with dominant granular mesangial IgA and C3 deposition on immunofluorescence, histopathologically indistinguishable from primary IgA nephropathy (Berger disease).

Hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis syndrome (HUVS, McDuffie syndrome) is characterized by chronic urticarial lesions persisting >24 to 48 hours that are burning or painful, marked hypocomplementemia (low C1q, C3, C4), and autoantibodies against C1q.

Skin biopsy in urticarial vasculitis demonstrates true leukocytoclastic vasculitis with postcapillary venular fibrinoid necrosis, endothelial swelling, and neutrophil karyorrhexis, contrasting with simple allergic wheals.

Severe pulmonary disease is the primary cause of mortality in HUVS, presenting with accelerated panacinar pulmonary emphysema and severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) in young adult non-smokers or smokers.

Supportive care with adequate hydration and simple analgesics suffices for mild pediatric IgA vasculitis, while systemic glucocorticoids relieve severe abdominal colic or articular pain without preventing chronic nephritis.

Severe crescentic IgA vasculitis nephritis or severe systemic HUVS (glomerulonephritis, severe ocular or pulmonary disease) requires high-dose systemic glucocorticoids combined with mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide, or rituximab.

topics.title: Anti-GBM disease
mustKnow: Anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) disease (Goodpasture disease) is an acute, severe autoimmune vasculitis caused by autoantibodies directed against the non-collagenous 1 (NC1) domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen [alpha3(IV)NC1].

The clinical presentation features rapidly progressive crescentic glomerulonephritis in nearly all patients, with concurrent life-threatening diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (pulmonary-renal syndrome, historically termed Goodpasture syndrome) occurring in 40% to 60%, heavily provoked by cigarette smoking, hydrocarbon inhalation, or respiratory infection.

Direct immunofluorescence of renal biopsy tissue reveals the pathognomonic finding: intense, unbroken, continuous, bright linear deposition of IgG (primarily IgG1 and IgG3) and C3 along the glomerular capillary basement membranes.

Light microscopy shows extensive, severe necrotizing glomerulonephritis with cellular crescents affecting >50% to 80% of glomeruli, which rapidly progress to circumferential fibrocellular crescents and irreversible global glomerulosclerosis if untreated.

'Double-positive' patients possess both circulating anti-GBM antibodies and ANCA (predominantly MPO-ANCA) in up to 20% to 30% of anti-GBM cases; they present acutely like severe anti-GBM disease but exhibit a higher long-term relapse rate characteristic of ANCA-associated vasculitis.

Immediate first-line triple therapy is mandatory: intensive therapeutic plasma exchange (daily 4-liter exchanges for 14 days or until anti-GBM titers are undetectable) combined with high-dose intravenous glucocorticoids and oral cyclophosphamide (2 mg/kg/day for 2 to 3 months).

Patients who present with anuria, 100% cellular crescents on biopsy, and are dialysis-dependent at presentation rarely recover renal function; however, if diffuse alveolar hemorrhage is present, aggressive plasma exchange and immunosuppression are still life-saving.

Unlike ANCA vasculitis or SLE, pure anti-GBM disease is a monophasic autoimmune illness with very low risk of late relapse once circulating antibodies are cleared, permitting discontinuation of cyclophosphamide after 2 to 3 months and steroid withdrawal within 6 to 9 months.

topics.title: Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis
mustKnow: Cryoglobulinemia is characterized by immunoglobulins that precipitate reversibly at temperatures below 37 degrees Celsius; Brouet classification stratifies into Type I (monoclonal Ig), Type II (monoclonal IgM with RF plus polyclonal IgG), and Type III (polyclonal IgM and IgG).

Brouet Type II mixed cryoglobulinemia accounts for >80% to 90% of cryoglobulinemic vasculitis cases, presenting with rheumatoid factor activity and driven predominantly by chronic Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection.
The classic Meltzer triad consists of palpable purpura (predominantly on lower extremities), profound fatigue, and arthralgias or non-erosive arthritis.

Serological testing reveals profound classical complement pathway consumption characterized by selectively depressed or undetectable serum C4 and low CH50, alongside normal or only mildly depressed C3 and high-titer RF.

Renal involvement affects 30% to 50% of patients, presenting as membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) with double-contour basement membrane duplications ('tram-track' appearance) and massive intraluminal cryoglobulin aggregates ('hyaline pseudothrombi').

Peripheral neuropathy occurs in 50% to 70% of patients, manifesting as painful sensory or sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy or mononeuritis multiplex caused by epineurial small-vessel cryoglobulin deposition and ischemia.

First-line therapy for HCV-associated mixed cryoglobulinemia is direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapy (e.g., sofosbuvir-based regimens for 12 weeks), which eradicates viral replication and induces clinical vasculitis remission.

For severe organ-threatening cryoglobulinemic vasculitis (rapidly progressive MPGN, digital gangrene, mononeuritis multiplex), immediate B-cell depletion with rituximab (375 mg/m2 weekly for 4 doses) combined with glucocorticoids and plasma exchange is prioritized.

topics.title: Behcet disease
mustKnow: Behcet disease (Silk Road disease) is a variable-vessel systemic vasculitis characterized by recurrent orogenital aphthosis, ocular inflammation, and distinctive inflammatory thrombotic involvement affecting both arteries and veins of all calibers.

The International Criteria for Behcet's Disease (ICBD, 2014) assign 2 points each to oral aphthosis, genital aphthosis, and ocular lesions, and 1 point each to skin lesions, vascular lesions, central nervous system involvement, and a positive pathergy test; a cumulative score >=4 points confirms diagnosis with high sensitivity (>94%).

Genetic susceptibility is strongly linked to the HLA-B51 allele (specifically HLA-B*5101), which is present in 50% to 80% of patients along the ancient Silk Road (Middle East, Turkey, Central Asia, Japan), conferring a 5- to 6-fold increased risk of developing Behcet disease.

The pathergy reaction is a non-specific cutaneous hyperreactivity test; intradermal puncture of the forearm with a sterile 20- to 22-gauge needle produces an erythematous papule or sterile pustule (>=2 mm diameter) surrounded by an erythematous halo within 24 to 48 hours.

Ocular involvement affects up to 50% to 70% of patients, characterized by acute recurrent episodes of non-granulomatous panuveitis, retinal vasculitis, and sterile hypopyon (a visible layer of white exudate pooling in the anterior chamber) which shifts with gravity, causing irreversible visual loss if untreated.

Vascular manifestations ('angio-Behcet') affect up to 40% of patients, with venous thrombosis (superficial thrombophlebitis, deep vein thrombosis, Budd-Chiari syndrome, and superior vena cava syndrome) being far more common than arterial disease; pulmonary artery aneurysms (PAA) are a classic arterial hallmark that carry high mortality from fatal hemoptysis upon rupture.

Neurological involvement ('neuro-Behcet', occurring in 5% to 10%) is stratified into parenchymal disease (brainstem-diencephalic encephalitis and meningoencephalitis with poor prognosis) and non-parenchymal disease (cerebral venous sinus thrombosis presenting with isolated raised intracranial pressure and papilledema).

Therapy for severe Behcet disease (posterior uveitis, pulmonary artery aneurysms, neuro-Behcet) requires high-dose systemic glucocorticoids combined with intravenous cyclophosphamide or monoclonal anti-TNF antibodies (infliximab, adalimumab); anticoagulation alone is dangerous in angio-Behcet because active pulmonary aneurysms can rupture into bronchi.

topics.title: Cogan syndrome and single organ vasculitis
mustKnow: Cogan syndrome is a rare variable-vessel vasculitis characterized by non-syphilitic interstitial keratitis (IK) and progressive sensorineural hearing loss with vestibular dysfunction (vertigo, ataxia, tinnitus) resembling Meniere disease.

Cardiovascular involvement occurs in 10% to 15% of Cogan syndrome patients, manifesting as severe ascending aortitis, aortic root dilatation leading to acute aortic regurgitation, coronary arteritis, and systemic vasculitis.

Early high-dose systemic glucocorticoids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day) combined with steroid-sparing agents (methotrexate, azathioprine, or anti-TNF infliximab) are critical in Cogan syndrome to prevent permanent, irreversible bilateral deafness.

Primary angiitis of the central nervous system (PACNS) is a single-organ vasculitis strictly confined to the brain and leptomeninges, presenting with chronic headache, encephalopathy, and multifocal ischemic strokes, with abnormal CSF in >90%.

Isolated cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis (hypersensitivity vasculitis) is a single-organ small-vessel vasculitis restricted to the skin, typically presenting with self-limiting palpable purpura following drug exposure or viral infection.

Isolated testicular vasculitis is a medium-vessel single-organ necrotizing vasculitis presenting with unilateral testicular pain and swelling, often mimicking a testicular neoplasm or torsion, diagnosed after orchiectomy without requiring systemic immunosuppression.

Isolated breast arteritis and isolated gastrointestinal vasculitis represent other localized single-organ vasculitides; long-term longitudinal monitoring is mandatory because up to 10% to 15% subsequently develop widespread systemic necrotizing vasculitis.

Brain biopsy remains the diagnostic gold standard for PACNS, demonstrating transmural granulomatous, lymphocytic, or necrotizing arteritis of parenchymal and leptomeningeal vessels while excluding infection and lymphoma.

topics.title: Relapsing polychondritis and VEXAS syndrome
mustKnow: Relapsing polychondritis is an episodic autoimmune disorder targeting cartilaginous structures, characterized by recurrent painful inflammation of ears, nose, larynx, trachea, joints, and eyes, targeting type II, IX, and XI collagen.

Auricular chondritis is the most specific hallmark, presenting with acute violaceous erythema and edema of the pinna that characteristically involves the cartilaginous helix and antihelix while strictly sparing the non-cartilaginous earlobe.

Nasal chondritis produces cartilage dissolution resulting in permanent saddle-nose deformity; laryngotracheal chondritis causes hoarseness, stridor, dynamic airway collapse, and represents the leading cause of disease-related mortality in up to 50%.

VEXAS syndrome (Vacuoles, E1 enzyme, X-linked, Autoinflammatory, Somatic) is an adult-onset monogenic autoinflammatory disorder caused by somatic mosaic missense mutations at codon p.Met41 in the X-linked UBA1 gene in hematopoietic stem cells.

VEXAS occurs almost exclusively in men older than 50 years, frequently misdiagnosed as refractory relapsing polychondritis, polyarteritis nodosa, or giant cell arteritis; bone marrow biopsy demonstrates pathognomonic cytoplasmic vacuoles in myeloid and erythroid precursor cells.

Clinical hallmarks of VEXAS syndrome include treatment-refractory relapsing chondritis (ear, nose), neutrophilic dermatoses (Sweet syndrome), periorbital edema, pulmonary infiltrates, deep vein thrombosis, and progressive macrocytic anemia and myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS).

VEXAS syndrome displays extreme refractoriness to conventional DMARDs and biologics, with high-dose glucocorticoid dependence; oral JAK inhibitors (ruxolitinib, upadacitinib) and hypomethylating agents (azacitidine) show significant clinical efficacy.

Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allogeneic HSCT) represents the only potentially curative definitive therapy for VEXAS syndrome, successfully eradicating the somatic UBA1-mutated clone in severe transfusion-dependent cases.

topics.title: Thromboangiitis obliterans and vasculitis mimics
mustKnow: Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease) is a non-atherosclerotic, segmental inflammatory vasculopathy affecting small- and medium-sized arteries and veins of the extremities, occurring almost exclusively in heavy tobacco smokers younger than 45 years.

Histopathology in Buerger disease reveals acute hypercellular, highly inflammatory intraluminal thrombi with microabscesses and multinucleated giant cells that preserve the internal elastic lamina and vessel architecture, distinguishing it from necrotizing arteritis.

Clinical hallmarks of Buerger disease include digital ischemia (Raynaud, rest pain, digital ulceration, gangrene), superficial migratory thrombophlebitis, and absent distal pulses; complete, permanent cessation of all tobacco and nicotine products is the only intervention that arrests disease progression.

Cholesterol atheroembolism (atheroembolic renal disease) results from rupture of atherosclerotic aortic plaques following vascular catheterization, anticoagulation, or thrombolysis; manifests with livedo reticularis, painful 'blue toes' with preserved peripheral pulses, acute renal failure, and transient eosinophilia.

Tissue biopsy in cholesterol atheroembolism demonstrates biconvex, needle-shaped 'cholesterol clefts' (empty spaces where intravascular cholesterol crystals dissolved during routine histological processing) surrounded by foreign-body giant cell inflammation.

Atrial myxoma (predominantly left atrial) is a classic systemic vasculitis mimicker: tumor embolization causes digital gangrene, cutaneous purpura, stroke, or retinal artery occlusion, while tumor IL-6 secretion produces fever, weight loss, arthralgias, elevated ESR, and false-positive autoantibodies.

Calciphylaxis (calcific uremic arteriolopathy) occurs primarily in end-stage renal disease on dialysis, characterized by mural medial calcification and intimal proliferation of small subcutaneous arterioles, producing exquisitely painful ischemic purpura progressing to black, necrotic eschars on adipose areas.

Levamisole-adulterated cocaine toxicity presents as an aggressive vasculitis mimic featuring painful, purpuric, retiform lesions with bullae that progress to necrosis on the ears, nose, and extremities; laboratory testing reveals agranulocytosis and striking dual seropositivity for p-ANCA (anti-MPO) and c-ANCA (anti-PR3).

topics.title: Monogenic autoinflammatory syndromes
mustKnow: Monogenic autoinflammatory syndromes are inherited disorders of the innate immune system characterized by unprovoked, recurrent episodes of systemic inflammation without high-titer autoantibodies or antigen-specific autoreactive T cells.

Familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) is caused by autosomal recessive MEFV mutations encoding pyrin; attacks last 12 to 72 hours with fever, peritonitis, pleuritis, and erysipelas-like rash, treated with daily lifelong oral colchicine to prevent fatal renal AA amyloidosis.

Cryopyrin-Associated Periodic Syndromes (CAPS) are autosomal dominant disorders caused by gain-of-function NLRP3 mutations, comprising FCAS, Muckle-Wells syndrome (urticaria, sensorineural deafness, amyloidosis), and NOMID/CINCA (aseptic meningitis, arthropathy), all responding dramatically to IL-1 blockade.

TNF Receptor-Associated Periodic Syndrome (TRAPS) is autosomal dominant caused by TNFRSF1A mutations (55-kDa TNF receptor), presenting with prolonged attacks lasting 1 to 3 weeks with migratory myalgias, monocytic fasciitis, periorbital edema, and high AA amyloidosis risk, treated with anakinra or canakinumab.

Hyper-IgD Syndrome / Mevalonate Kinase Deficiency (HIDS/MKD) is autosomal recessive caused by MVK mutations, presenting with attacks every 4 to 6 weeks lasting 3 to 7 days, often triggered by childhood vaccinations, featuring cervical lymphadenopathy, mouth ulcers, and elevated IgD/IgA.

Blau syndrome is an autosomal dominant pediatric autoinflammatory granulomatous disorder caused by gain-of-function NOD2 (CARD15) mutations, characterized by the clinical triad of granulomatous polyarthritis, panuveitis, and camptodactyly with tan papular rash.

PAPA syndrome (Pyogenic Arthritis, Pyoderma gangrenosum, and Acne) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by PSTPIP1 (CD2BP1) mutations, leading to hyperphosphorylation and uninhibited binding to pyrin, driving sterile neutrophilic articular and cutaneous destruction.

Type I interferonopathies (e.g., Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome, STING-associated vasculopathy with onset in infancy [SAVI]) are monogenic disorders characterized by constitutive upregulation of type I interferons, presenting with microangiopathy, chilblains, pulmonary fibrosis, and stroke, responsive to oral JAK inhibitors.

topics.title: Macrophage activation syndrome and HLH
mustKnow: Macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) is a life-threatening form of secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (sHLH) complicating systemic autoimmune diseases, most commonly systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (sJIA), adult-onset Still disease (AOSD), and systemic lupus erythematosus.

Pathophysiology involves defective cytotoxic T-lymphocyte and natural killer (NK) cell cytolytic function (impaired perforin and granzyme B release), resulting in failure to clear antigen-presenting cells and sustained, uncontrolled hyperactivation of CD8+ T cells and macrophages producing a lethal cytokine storm.

The 2016 EULAR/ACR/PRINTO classification criteria for MAS in systemic JIA require a febrile patient with confirmed or suspected sJIA and serum ferritin >684 ng/mL plus at least 2 of 4 laboratory criteria: platelet count <=181,000/microL, AST >48 U/L, triglycerides >156 mg/dL, or fibrinogen <=360 mg/dL.

A sudden, paradoxical drop in erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) in a severely ill, febrile Still disease or lupus patient is a hallmark clinical warning sign of MAS, caused by rapid consumptive hypofibrinogenemia and hepatic synthetic failure.

Extreme hyperferritinemia (frequently >10,000 to >50,000 ng/mL) is the single most sensitive diagnostic and prognostic biomarker of active MAS, directly reflecting massive activated macrophage iron storage and secretion.

Bone marrow aspirate or trephine biopsy demonstrates hemophagocytosis: mature, non-malignant CD68+ macrophages engulfing erythrocytes, leukocytes, platelets, and erythroblasts; however, hemophagocytosis is non-specific and its absence on initial marrow examination never excludes MAS.

First-line emergency therapy requires immediate high-dose intravenous pulse methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg/day up to 1 g/day for 3 days), combined with high-dose intravenous or subcutaneous anakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist, 8 to 10 mg/kg/day) or cyclosporine A (2 to 5 mg/kg/day).

Emapalumab, a fully human IgG1 monoclonal antibody targeting and neutralizing interferon-gamma (IFN-gamma), is FDA-approved for primary HLH and highly effective as rescue therapy in refractory MAS/sHLH with life-threatening multiorgan failure.

topics.title: Sarcoidosis systemic manifestations
mustKnow: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disorder of unknown etiology characterized by the formation of non-caseating (non-necrotizing) epithelioid cell granulomas in multiple organs and tissues, with pulmonary and intrathoracic lymph node involvement occurring in >90% of patients.

Lofgren syndrome is an acute, self-limiting clinical presentation of sarcoidosis consisting of the classic triad of bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL), acute migratory periarthritis (predominantly involving both ankles), and erythema nodosum, which carries an excellent prognosis with spontaneous remission in >80% to 90%.

Heerfordt syndrome (uveoparotid fever) is a rare specific acute presentation characterized by the tetrad of anterior uveitis, parotid gland enlargement, low-grade fever, and cranial nerve palsy (most commonly unilateral or bilateral seventh [facial] nerve lower motor neuron palsy).

The Scadding radiographic staging system classifies thoracic sarcoidosis on chest radiographs into five stages: Stage 0 (normal radiograph), Stage I (bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy without parenchymal infiltrates), Stage II (BHL plus pulmonary parenchymal infiltrates), Stage III (pulmonary infiltrates without BHL), and Stage IV (advanced fibrotic pulmonary disease with volume loss and honeycombing).

Histopathological examination of affected tissues demonstrates well-formed, compact non-caseating granulomas composed of CD4+ T lymphocytes and epithelioid histiocytes, with multinucleated Langhans giant cells containing characteristic intracytoplasmic inclusions: asteroid bodies (star-shaped) and Schaumann bodies (concentric laminated basophilic calcifications).

Disordered calcium metabolism occurs in up to 10% to 20% of sarcoidosis patients (hypercalcemia in 10%, hypercalciuria in 30%), caused by unregulated extrarenal 1-alpha-hydroxylation of 25-hydroxyvitamin D into active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol) by pulmonary alveolar and granuloma macrophages, independent of PTH control.

Cardiac sarcoidosis is an underdiagnosed, life-threatening manifestation presenting with high-grade atrioventricular heart block, malignant ventricular tachyarrhythmias, congestive cardiomyopathy, and sudden cardiac death; cardiac MRI demonstrates patchy epicardial or mid-wall late gadolinium enhancement, and 18F-FDG PET-CT identifies active myocardial inflammatory metabolic activity.

Systemic glucocorticoids (oral prednisone 20 to 40 mg daily) are the first-line therapy for symptomatic or organ-threatening sarcoidosis (cardiac, neurologic, ocular, severe hypercalcemia, progressive pulmonary disease); for steroid-refractory disease or steroid-sparing maintenance, methotrexate (10 to 20 mg weekly), azathioprine, or anti-TNF monoclonal antibodies (infliximab) provide proven efficacy.

topics.title: Amyloidosis in rheumatology
mustKnow: Amyloidosis encompasses a heterogeneous group of protein-folding disorders in which soluble precursor proteins aggregate into insoluble, unbranched 7.5 to 10 nm cross-beta-sheet fibrils that deposit extracellularly in organs and tissues, causing progressive organ dysfunction.

Histopathological diagnosis requires tissue biopsy (abdominal subcutaneous fat aspirate [sensitivity 70% to 80%], minor salivary gland, rectal, or involved organ) demonstrating pathognomonic bright apple-green birefringence under cross-polarized light microscopy following Congo red staining.

AL (primary) amyloidosis is caused by a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia producing monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains (lambda in 75%, kappa in 25%); clinical hallmarks include nephrotic syndrome, restrictive cardiomyopathy with low ECG voltage, hepatomegaly, macroglossia (pathognomonic, in 15%), and periorbital ecchymoses ('raccoon eyes') caused by amyloid vascular fragility.

AA (reactive/secondary) amyloidosis is driven by chronic, sustained systemic inflammation (rheumatoid arthritis, spondyloarthritis, familial Mediterranean fever, bronchiectasis, chronic osteomyelitis) stimulating hepatic overproduction of acute-phase serum amyloid A (SAA); renal amyloid deposition causes heavy proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome, and end-stage renal disease.

Transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR) is caused by misfolded transthyretin (TTR), occurring as wild-type ATTR (ATTRwt, formerly senile systemic amyloidosis, affecting elderly men with restrictive cardiomyopathy and carpal tunnel syndrome) or hereditary mutant ATTR (ATTRv, e.g., Val122Ile or Val30Met, causing familial amyloid polyneuropathy and cardiomyopathy).

Cardiac amyloidosis features concentric biventricular wall thickening with small ventricular cavities, severe diastolic dysfunction with restrictive filling pattern, low QRS voltage on ECG despite thickened myocardium on echocardiogram (pathognomonic voltage-to-mass discordance), and apical sparing of longitudinal strain ('cherry on top' pattern).

Bone scintigraphy using 99mTc-pyrophosphate (99mTc-PYP) or 99mTc-DPD demonstrates intense myocardial tracer uptake (Perugini grade 2 or 3) in ATTR cardiac amyloidosis, enabling non-biopsy diagnosis of ATTR cardiomyopathy when monoclonal free light chains are excluded.

Disease-modifying therapies target precursor proteins: AL amyloidosis is treated with anti-plasma cell regimens (daratumumab, bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, dexamethasone [Dara-CyBorD]); AA amyloidosis requires aggressive suppression of underlying inflammation; and ATTR is treated with the oral TTR kinetic stabilizer tafamidis (61 mg daily) or TTR gene-silencing siRNA/antisense oligonucleotides (patisiran, vutrisiran, inotersen).

topics.title: Septic arthritis and prosthetic joint infection
mustKnow: Acute bacterial septic arthritis is a destructive orthopedic and rheumatologic emergency resulting from hematogenous seeding, direct inoculation, or contiguous spread into the vascular synovial membrane, capable of causing irreversible cartilage degradation within 24 to 48 hours via chondrocyte chondrolysis and bacterial protease release.

Staphylococcus aureus is the overall most frequent causative bacterial pathogen across all age groups in native joint septic arthritis (responsible for 50% to 60% of non-gonococcal cases), with methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) increasingly prevalent; other major pathogens include Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B), and gram-negative bacilli in elderly or immunocompromised hosts.

The classical clinical presentation of non-gonococcal septic arthritis is acute, severe, monoarticular joint pain with swelling, warmth, erythema, and marked restriction of both active and passive motion; the knee is the most commonly involved joint (>50% of cases), followed by the hip, shoulder, ankle, and wrist.

Diagnostic arthrocentesis must be performed urgently prior to antibiotic administration: synovial fluid analysis characteristically reveals marked purulence with leukocyte count >50,000/microL (often >100,000/microL) and >75% to 90% polymorphonuclear neutrophils, elevated lactate, and markedly depressed synovial glucose (<50% of blood glucose).

Synovial fluid Gram stain is positive in 50% to 75% of non-gonococcal septic arthritis, and aerobic/anaerobic cultures identify the pathogen in >80% to 90%; simultaneous blood cultures should be drawn in all patients and are positive in up to 50% of hematogenous infections.

Empirical intravenous antibiotic therapy must be initiated immediately after arthrocentesis: vancomycin (15 to 20 mg/kg every 8 to 12 hours) targeting MRSA, combined with a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone 2 g daily) or antipseudomonal beta-lactam if gram-negative bacilli are suspected, adjusted upon definitive culture and sensitivities.

Prompt joint decompression is an absolute mandatory pillar of therapy: repeated daily needle aspirations, arthroscopic drainage and debridement, or open arthrotomy (mandatory for septic arthritis of the hip or anatomically complex joints), ensuring complete evacuation of purulent exudate and reduction of intra-articular pressure.

Total antibiotic duration is typically 3 to 4 weeks for uncomplicated non-gonococcal septic arthritis, initiated intravenously and transitioned to targeted oral therapy once clinical inflammation has resolved and inflammatory markers (CRP) normalize.

topics.title: Viral and post-infectious arthritis
mustKnow: Parvovirus B19 arthritis classically causes a symmetrical polyarthritis mimicking early RA in young adult females; anti-B19 IgM establishes diagnosis while PCR detects viral DNA.

Chikungunya alphavirus manifests with abrupt high fever, maculopapular rash, and crippling polyarthralgia/polyarthritis persisting chronologically >3 months in up to 30-40% of patients as chronic post-chikungunya rheumatism.

Hepatitis B virus prodrome presents with serum sickness-like syndrome (fever, urticarial rash, symmetrical polyarthritis, hypocomplementemia with low C3/C4) mediated by circulating HBsAg-anti-HBs immune complexes.

Hepatitis C virus causes both non-deforming rheumatoid-like polyarthritis and mixed cryoglobulinemic vasculitis (type II cryoglobulinemia with monoclonal IgM kappa against polyclonal IgG RF activity).
Ross River and Barmah Forest alphaviruses endemic to Australia/Oceania produce epidemic polyarthritis with ankle/wrist predilection accompanied by maculopapular trunk eruptions.

Zika flavivirus infection causes self-limited mild arthralgia/non-purulent conjunctivitis/maculopapular exanthem, differentiated from Dengue by absence of severe leukopenia or hemorrhagic thrombocytopenia.

Post-streptococcal reactive arthritis (PSRA) develops within 10-14 days post-Streptococcal pharyngitis, non-migratory, responds poorly to high-dose aspirin/NSAIDs (unlike acute rheumatic fever migratory polyarthritis), and lacks Jones major cardiac/chorea criteria.

Rubella wild-type infection or RA27/3 attenuated vaccine administration triggers transient acute morning stiffness and symmetrical small joint synovitis in 15-30% of adult women resolving within 2-4 weeks.

topics.title: Fibromyalgia and chronic widespread pain
mustKnow: 2016 revised ACR diagnostic criteria define Fibromyalgia by Widespread Pain Index (WPI) >= 7 and Symptom Severity Scale (SSS) >= 5, OR WPI 4-6 and SSS >= 9, with generalized pain in >= 4 of 5 defined body regions present >= 3 months.

Central sensitization in fibromyalgia is neurobiologically characterized by decreased descending serotonergic/noradrenergic inhibitory pain pathways and elevated excitatory CSF substance P, glutamate, and nerve growth factor (NGF).

Functional MRI during pain processing demonstrates hyperactivation of the insula, anterior cingulate cortex, and somatosensory cortex at low stimulus pressures, confirming tactile and pressure allodynia.

Pregabalin (alpha-2-delta ligand decreasing presynaptic calcium-dependent excitatory neurotransmitter release) is approved at target doses of 300-450 mg/day divided twice daily for fibromyalgia symptom relief.

Duloxetine (dual serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, SNRI) administered at 60 mg/day significantly reduces central chronic widespread pain and depressive affect independently of baseline depression scores.
Milnacipran (potent selective SNRI with higher relative norepinephrine selectivity) dosed at 100-200 mg/day improves patient global impression of change, fatigue, and widespread pain scores.

Non-pharmacologic management carries highest EULAR grade of recommendation, specifically graded low-impact aerobic exercise (walking, swimming, cycling >= 150 minutes/week) and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT).
Opioids and systemic corticosteroids show zero clinical efficacy in central pain processing in fibromyalgia and are strongly contraindicated due to hyperalgesia and dependence risks.

topics.title: Regional and soft tissue rheumatism
mustKnow: Rotator cuff tendinopathy most commonly involves the supraspinatus tendon at the critical hypovascular zone 1 cm proximal to its greater tuberosity insertion; Neer and Hawkins-Kennedy impingement tests elicit subacromial pain.

Lateral epicondylitis ('tennis elbow') involves microtrauma and angiofibroblastic tendinosis predominantly at the origin of the extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) tendon, elicited by resisted third-digit extension (Maudsley test) and resisted wrist extension.
Medial epicondylitis ('golfer's elbow') targets the common flexor tendon and pronator teres origin, provoked by resisted wrist flexion and pronation with elbow extended.

De Quervain tenosynovitis involves stenosing tenosynovitis of the first dorsal extensor compartment enclosing the abductor pollicis longus (APL) and extensor pollicis brevis (EPB) tendons; pathognomonic Eichhoff / Finkelstein test reproduces pain.

Trochanteric pain syndrome (greater trochanteric pain syndrome, GTPS) is primarily caused by gluteus medius and minimus tendinopathy or tear rather than isolated trochanteric bursitis; pain is provoked by single-leg standing >= 30 seconds.

Adhesive capsulitis ('frozen shoulder') progresses through freezing, frozen, and thawing stages, characterized pathologically by dense glenohumeral capsular contracture and loss of both active AND passive external rotation (>50% restriction).

Pes anserine bursitis/tendinopathy causes focal tenderness 5 cm distal to the medial tibial joint line at the conjoined insertion of sartorius, gracilis, and semitendinosus (SGS) tendons, common in elderly obese females with knee osteoarthritis.

Plantar fasciitis presents with intense heel pain upon the first morning weight-bearing steps, localized to the medial calcaneal tuberosity insertion with windlass test exacerbating pain on passive first metatarsophalangeal dorsiflexion.

topics.title: Ocular manifestations of rheumatic disease
mustKnow: Anterior uveitis (acute anterior uveitis, AAU) is the most common extra-articular feature of axial spondyloarthritis (HLA-B27 positive in >80%), characteristically presenting as acute, unilateral, alternating, painful red eye with photophobia.

Necrotizing anterior scleritis with inflammation presents with severe boring ocular pain radiating to the temple/forehead; >50% have underlying systemic necrotizing vasculitis (GPA, PAN) or destructive RA requiring urgent systemic cyclophosphamide or biologic therapy.

Scleromalacia perforans (necrotizing scleritis without inflammation) occurs classically in long-standing seropositive erosive rheumatoid arthritis, manifesting as painless scleral thinning exposing dark bluish-black underlying uvea without active hyperemic congestion.

Peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK) is a sight-threatening crescent-shaped corneal stromal melt at the limbus mediated by collagenase and immune-complex vasculitis of the anterior ciliary circulation, highly associated with active GPA and severe RA.

Uveitis in juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is typically chronic, bilateral, non-granulomatous, and clinically 'silent' (asymptomatic, white quiet eye) in oligoarticular ANA-positive young females, necessitating scheduled slit-lamp surveillance to avert band keratopathy.

Retinal vasculitis presenting with branch retinal artery or vein occlusion with classic 'frosted branch angiitis' or retinal periarteritis occurs prominently in systemic lupus erythematosus, Behçet disease, and GPA.

Behçet disease causes recurrent explosive bilateral panuveitis with shifting, hypopyon that resolves spontaneously without posterior synechiae scarring, requiring infliximab, adalimumab, or interferon-alpha to preserve vision.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) classically causes retro-orbital pseudotumor / inflammatory orbital mass leading to proptosis, diplopia, compressive optic neuropathy, and nasolacrimal duct obstruction in up to 15-20% of patients.

topics.title: Neurological manifestations of rheumatic disease
mustKnow: Neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus (NPSLE) classification encompasses 19 case definitions by ACR; diffuse psychiatric/cognitive manifestations are linked with anti-ribosomal P antibodies, while lupus psychosis correlates with CSF pleocytosis/elevated IgG index.

Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) co-occurs with SLE and Sjögren syndrome; mediated by pathogenic IgG antibodies targeting aquaporin-4 (AQP4) water channels on astrocyte foot processes, causing longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (LETM >= 3 vertebral segments).

Primary angiitis of the central nervous system (PACNS) is restricted to brain/spinal leptomeningeal parenchymal arteries <500 µm, diagnosed definitively by high-resolution vessel wall MRI and stereotactic brain-leptomeningeal biopsy showing granulomatous or lymphocytic vasculitis.
